name: Policy
title: Why ICE Is Quietly Buying Up Private Detention Centers - TIME
description:
The latest plan, according to ICE sources and officials with private prison companies, is for ICE to take over private detention facilities while building new ones alongside them.
Officials with CoreCivic and the GEO Group, the two biggest owners of private ICE detention facilities, have both discussed selling more sites to the U.S. government.
The company also acknowledged in its statement that it has been negotiating with ICE regarding "additional" sales of its detention facilities.
Immigration advocates say the Trump Administration is buying private detention centers to clamp down on oversight of what goes on inside them.
Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former senior ICE official, said one of the key reasons so many problems persist at ICE detention centers is the reduction of oversight from internal watchdog offices.
text:
The announcement didn’t make much news initially. CoreCivic, one of the largest private prison operators in the country, announced early last month that the U.S. government was buying two of its facilities for $1.5 billion. Both sites are set to be used the same way they have for years—as detention centers for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The deal was the latest twist in the Trump Administration’s fumbling efforts to dramatically expand the number of migrants it can hold at once. Over the last year and a half, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has veered from planning to reopen more than a dozen shuttered prisons, to housing thousands of migrants in sprawling tent facilities, to retrofitting nearly a dozen commercial warehouses into new detention centers. Despite billions of dollars spent, each strategy has largely fallen by the wayside, stymied by legal and political headwinds.

The latest plan, according to ICE sources and officials with private prison companies, is for ICE to take over private detention facilities while building new ones alongside them. Officials with CoreCivic and the GEO Group, the two biggest owners of private ICE detention facilities, have both discussed selling more sites to the U.S. government.

ICE is paying CoreCivic $739.2 million for the Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego and $732.6 million for the California City Detention Facility in Kern County. Both facilities have been in operation for more than a decade and together hold a daily average of more than 1,200 immigrants, according to the latest ICE data. CoreCivic will continue managing these facilities.

The company also acknowledged in its statement that it has been negotiating with ICE regarding "additional" sales of its detention facilities. GEO Group, said during its earnings call in May that ICE had been in touch with the company about purchasing some of its 19 detention facilities.

Immigration advocates say the Trump Administration is buying private detention centers to clamp down on oversight of what goes on inside them. “Once the facility is entirely owned by the federal government, that limits the ability of state and local inspectors to try to gain some insight as to what is happening in there, or seek changes to conditions that may be potentially violative of people's rights," Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, tells TIME.

As immigration enforcement operations have surged nationwide since Trump’s second inauguration, several states have passed laws empowering local officials to inspect privately-owned detention facilities. So far, efforts by private firms to shrug off these laws aren’t working. Soon after California passed a health inspection law in 2024 targeting privately-owned prisons, GEO Group challenged the law in court, but the case was eventually dismissed by a federal judge. GEO Group is battling similar cases in Colorado, New Jersey and Washington state.

“As some blue states are considering more active involvement in oversight of facilities, I think the logical solution to much of that is federal ownership of the facilities,” George Zoley, CEO of GEO Group, said during the company's earnings call in May. Zoley made clear his thinking on the advantage of federal ownership was all about reducing “unprecedented” lawsuits and oversight. He claimed that transferring the private facilities to the federal government would provide "stronger protections" under the Supremacy Clause in the Constitution.

Since the beginning of the second Trump administration, ICE has set a goal of doubling its detention capacity to more than 100,000 beds by the end of 2025, according to an internal document reported by the Washington Post. That goal has yet to be achieved seven months into 2026. White House border czar Tom Homan conceded earlier this month that ICE currently has "about 70,000 beds" and that he is pushing for more.

The agency's original plan was to build makeshift "soft-sided" detention facilities—tents, essentially—on military bases. That plan was quietly halted after the largest soft-sided facility at the Fort Bliss military base in Texas reported three deaths of detained immigrants and dozens of federal detention-standard deficiencies, according to an internal ICE review. Last summer, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wrote in a letter to Rep. Herb Conaway, a New Jersey Democrat, that similar tent facilities were being considered at other military bases, including Camp Atterbury in Indiana and Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst in New Jersey. So far, no such tent facilities have been built.

ICE then decided in January to execute Plan B: purchasing 11 commercial warehouses for $1 billion and converting them into detention facilities. The agency was quickly hit with eight lawsuits from local and state governments over the environmental impact of those projects on nearby communities. The New York Times reported that, following these lawsuits, ICE is planning to sell or give away seven of the 11 warehouses. It is unclear whether the agency will continue to move forward on its plan for the remaining four.

A former senior ICE official familiar with the agency’s efforts to expand detention capacity and granted anonymity to speak freely said that some of the warehouses ICE purchased had structural issues that may have prevented them from meeting federal detention standards. “Just because it was a quick way to politicize what the government wanted to do, it doesn't mean it was a well thought-out plan,” the former official added.

Now, there are signs ICE is laying the groundwork to execute Plan C: renting or purchasing existing facilities, while building new ones alongside them. The latest draft government contract revealed that ICE is planning to build additional detention units in as many as 14 locations across the United States, including the Virgin Islands and Guantanamo Bay. The potential locations include a mix of facilities already in use and ones that ICE shut down more than a decade ago; it is unclear whether the agency plans to build additional facilities at all 14 sites.

Reichlin-Melnick says ICE’s latest plan shows it’s leaning toward permanent brick-and-mortar structures, having abandoned the idea of expanding capacity through tents. Yet he is skeptical this latest effort will succeed, given the logistical costs of transporting detainees to facilities scattered so far apart. "Even with the money ICE has right now, it would cause them to burn through their funds very quickly. So I'm skeptical that all 14 of these facilities will be built out to the extent suggested," he added.

ICE's latest move to purchase detention centers from private contractors comes against the backdrop of a renewed push in deportation operations nationwide. According to ICE data, the agency arrested more than 39,000 people in June, the most arrests in a single month in the agency’s history. The rapid increase in arrests also drove up the total number of people in ICE custody to 65,765 — one of the highest levels this year. The influx of detainees is straining resources in ICE facilities nationwide, which have long reported overcrowding and a lack of adequate medical resources and legal representation.

Despite public pressure, ICE continues to instruct its private contractors to disregard state laws in its latest procurement documents. According to a draft contract published on July 10, ICE states that local or state laws and regulations "shall not apply" to private contractors while they are housing detainees, language that had appeared before, in a contract ICE signed with GEO Group for the Washington state facility in March, while that lawsuit was still ongoing. WIRED was first to report the language in the draft contract.

Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former senior ICE official, said one of the key reasons so many problems persist at ICE detention centers is the reduction of oversight from internal watchdog offices. The Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, created by Congress in 2020 to investigate facilities that fall short of detention standards, and the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, which protects the civil rights of detained immigrants, were both dismantled under Kristi Noem's leadership.

"Not only are there reduced people in the facilities looking for problems, there is also a lack of interest in making sure that the facilities are performing to the standards," Trickler-McNulty said.

The only remaining ICE office that conducts routine inspections, the Office of Detention Oversight, has been conducting fewer inspections than under previous administrations. A CBS News analysis found that 15 of the 45 detention facilities holding 500 or more people hadn't been inspected in over 12 months — a gap that experts say weakens internal mechanisms for holding contractors accountable.

description:
We are pleased to finally share our new Young Person’s Key Guide: Finding your way as a young person in the asylum and immigration system.

In particular, a huge thank you to PAFRAS and the young people for their invaluable contribution and heartfelt guidance for other young people going through the asylum system.

Since 2021, the situation for young people in the asylum system has also changed in important ways.
text:
We are pleased to finally share our new Young Person’s Key Guide: Finding your way as a young person in the asylum and immigration system.

This guide has been written for children and young people who are in the UK without a parent or carer, and who are trying to understand the asylum and immigration system. Some parts may also be useful for young people who are here with family, or for adults supporting young people through the process.

The guide builds on the groundbreaking Young Asylum Guide, and brings this work into the main Right to Remain Toolkit. It has been written in collaboration with Social Workers Without Borders, and shaped by the knowledge, experience and care of organisations, practitioners and young people themselves. In particular, a huge thank you to PAFRAS and the young people for their invaluable contribution and heartfelt guidance for other young people going through the asylum system.

We explain the history of the Young Asylum Guide and why we have made these changes in more detail here.

This is the first version of the Young Person’s Key Guide. As with the Right to Remain Toolkit, it is a living document that belongs to all of us and will continue to change and grow with the knowledge, experience and feedback of the communities and people who use it.

If you have feedback, suggestions or updates, please contact Ally Swadling, our Lead Legal Education Officer, at ally@righttoremain.org.uk

Why this guide matters

The asylum and immigration system is confusing for everyone. For young people, it can be especially overwhelming. Young people are forced to navigate a system that is hostile, isolating and difficult to understand, during a time we can all remember – when our bodies and minds are changing quickly, when we are learning what the world means, where we fit, who we can trust, and who we want to become.

Since 2021, the situation for young people in the asylum system has also changed in important ways. In particular, there has been a huge increase in age disputes with more children being treated as adults or going through difficult age assessment processes. The guide tries to respond to these realities.

We know that childhood and young adulthood are not just stages we simply pass through. What happens during these years shapes our confidence, safety, relationships, education, health and sense of belonging, long into adult life. For young people going through the asylum and immigration system, these experiences are happening in a new country, often while they are separated from family, learning a new language, missing home and everything home can mean, trying to understand unfamiliar systems, and waiting for decisions that affect their whole future.

Young people may also be watching friends and peers move through ordinary milestones, like school, college, work, family life and independence. Some of those peers may also be in the asylum or immigration system whose situations may feel similar to their own, but they may still experience wildly different waiting times, different levels of support, different allowances, and different responses from adults and services.

It is hard to swallow, at any age, how unfair and arbitrary the system can be. But it can be especially painful during such a formative time of life, when young people are trying to understand themselves, their place in the world, and what kind of future is possible.

In the opening message to young people reading the Key Guide, we write something that is worth repeating here:

You deserve safety, care, and the chance to enjoy life as a young person. Sadly, not everyone in the system will see this or treat you fairly. That is not your fault. You are not alone. Many others have been through the same process and found ways to keep going. Stay strong, ask for support, and remember your voice matters.

What the guide covers

The Young Person’s Key guide is practical. It explains the asylum process, but it also helps young people understand the people, organisations and decisions they may come across along the way.

It includes sections on:

people and organisations you might meet, and what decisions they can and cannot make

what to expect from important people like lawyers, social workers, Personal Advisers, interpreters and advocates

what happens when you first claim asylum

what to do if the Home Office or local authority says you are over 18

what to do if you are under 18 and placed in a hotel for adults

what happens during an age assessment, and what to do if you want to challenge one and finding a way forward if your age is not accepted (this has been written to complement the incredible work of Childhood First Age Assessment toolkit for practitioners and young people)

what happens in interviews, evidence forms and Home Office decision-making

what can happen after a decision, whether that decision is positive or negative

what happens if your asylum claim is refused, including appeals and other legal challenges

your rights in the UK, including education, health, work, volunteering and bank accounts

interacting with police and immigration officers

racism, hate crime, reporting and immigration detention

care and support from Children’s Services, including where you might live, meetings, turning 18, and care leaver support

How to use your voice in meetings

other immigration issues that may matter, including settlement, citizenship, family and private life, medical or human rights applications, and voluntary return

Moving the guide into the main Toolkit also means that every page can be translated (use the Google Translate bar in the top left hand corner) and links to the main Toolkit throughout.

Built from young people’s experiences

One of the first sections of the guide shares messages from young people who have worked with PAFRAS, a grassroots organisation based in Leeds, and who have already been through the asylum process.

They spoke about waiting, loneliness, uncertainty, learning English, missing family, trying to understand letters, and not always knowing who to ask for help. Their advice to other young people is practical and powerful: ask questions, keep documents safe, ask for an interpreter if you need one, and remember that you are not alone.

They also remind us of something very important: even when life may be safer in the UK, the asylum process can still be difficult, frightening and isolating but there can be hope, strength and power found in community and connection.

For young people, and for the adults supporting them

As with the whole Right to Remain Toolkit, this guide is not a passive resource. It is not just a link to share and then leave someone to work through alone.

Sit down with young people and read sections together. Use it to give legal support. Use it to prepare for appointments, understand letters, make plans, ask questions, and think about what might happen next.

The guide is most useful when it is used alongside people. As we keep saying at Right to Remain: solidarity is a verb!

name: Human Rights
title: We are US civil rights lawyers. Trump's policies have driven us to seek justice internationally
authors: Guardian staff, Thomas Becker, Antonio Romanucci
description:
We are constitutional law, civil rights, and human rights scholars and practitioners who have spent decades litigating government abuse cases in the United States.
Together with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, the commission is the bedrock of the hemisphere’s human rights system.
Condemnation by the commission has directly led to policy changes by countries, including the United States.
The international community has sharply criticized the United States’ treatment of immigrants.
A body that has historically held the hemisphere’s most authoritarian governments to account will now scrutinize the United States.
text:
We are constitutional law, civil rights, and human rights scholars and practitioners who have spent decades litigating government abuse cases in the United States. Despite the US legal system’s flaws, our work – from securing a record civil settlement for George Floyd’s family to holding Bolivia’s ex-president accountable in US federal court for the massacre of Indigenous protesters – has demonstrated that US courts can reign in state power and provide a path to accountability. But this pathway is narrowing.

As Donald Trump attacks the courts, weaponizes the Department of Justice, and targets attorneys who challenge his administration, we have been forced to seek justice beyond our borders.

Earlier this year, we requested a thematic hearing at the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) on the United States’s violent suppression of protests against federal immigration policies. Never before had the commission granted such a hearing, but the extraordinary nature of the Trump administration’s actions – including allegations of excessive and lethal force against peaceful protesters, attacks on journalists and legal observers, and racial profiling and surveillance – warrants international scrutiny. On 4 August, the commission will hold that hearing.

The IACHR is unfamiliar to most Americans. Together with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, the commission is the bedrock of the hemisphere’s human rights system. For decades, it has served as a safeguard against authoritarianism and State repression in the region, providing an avenue for victims when domestic institutions have failed. While the United States claims it is not bound by the Inter-American System’s norms, it remains subject to the commission’s oversight under the American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man. Condemnation by the commission has directly led to policy changes by countries, including the United States.

The IACHR typically convenes sessions of hearings three times per year, rotating the location between countries in the region. Fittingly, ours will be held in Washington DC, just two blocks from the White House.

Among those participating will be counsel for the family of Renee Good, who was shot and killed in her car by an ICE agent during a Minneapolis demonstration. Following the tragic killing of Good, the then Department of Homeland Security secretary, Kristi Noem, characterized Good’s actions as “domestic terrorism”. Good’s counsel will also speak on behalf of the dozens of victims in Chicago he represents injured at protests and denied basic rights in detention – including access to food, medicine, and lawyers. Also testifying will be the Rev David Black, who was shot in the head with a pepper ball by a federal agent at a protest outside Chicago. In response, Gregory Bovino, who was serving as US Customs and Border’s “commander-at-large”, said the shooting “was absolutely in line with policy, and I applaud [the agents]”.

Renee Good and the Rev Black are only two of the hundreds of protesters and bystanders who have been injured amid demonstrations against Trump’s remarkably cruel immigration policies. On his inauguration day, Trump signed a series of xenophobic executive orders, including the “Protecting the American People Against Invasion” order. Within days, he deployed federal agents to carry out paramilitary-style raids across US cities. Families have been torn apart and thrown into detention centers or sent to third countries. Everyday Americans watched agents abduct, beat and shoot unarmed migrants. Only weeks ago, separate violent ICE operations resulted in three more deaths.

The international community has sharply criticized the United States’ treatment of immigrants. United Nations high commissioner Volker Türk said he was “astounded by the now-routine abuse and denigration of migrants and refugees”, while the United Nations committee on the elimination of racial discrimination expressed alarm over what it called the “systematic use of racial profiling” by ICE and “[r]acist hate speech by political leaders, including the President”.

Such condemnation is entirely justified, but even those who support the administration’s immigration agenda should be deeply concerned by attacks on those who protest it. Today’s target may be anti-ICE protesters. Tomorrow it could be advocates for climate justice, gun rights, abortion or labor rights. Freedom of assembly and freedom of speech are cornerstones of any functioning democracy. When they are under attack, other freedoms quickly fall.

The upcoming hearing before the commission is both extraordinary and symbolic. A body that has historically held the hemisphere’s most authoritarian governments to account will now scrutinize the United States. As the Trump administration weakens domestic checks on power, international oversight has become not only relevant. It may be our last chance to stop the backsliding that threatens our democracy.

text:
Robert “Bob” Peck, of South Portland, is suing the U.S. government, claiming that two Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents violated his First and Fourth Amendment rights while he recorded their activities during a surge in ICE activity in Maine in January. The government has 60 days to respond to the suit.

It’s the first suit filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) against the U.S. government for the actions of federal agents against legal observers during the ICE surge in January, according to David Webbert, Peck’s lawyer.

Peck filed the initial notice of claim eight days after two unidentified federal agents came to his car window and threatened to arrest and harm him on Jan. 22 after Peck followed the officers from a field office in Scarborough, he said.

He had to wait six months after notifying before filing the suit to give the U.S. government time to respond, the typical protocol in cases filed under the FTCA. Since then, Webbert has been in occasional communication with lawyers for the U.S. attorney general, first sending information about the damage requests and later negotiating the terms of the confidential release of the identities of the two masked agents.

Webbert intends to serve the two agents as soon as they are named in an effort to get the ball rolling. They will each have 60 days to respond to the suit.

While he was waiting for the six-month period to elapse, Peck filed a civil complaint in June under the state’s civil rights act, accusing the two unidentified federal immigration agents of violating his First Amendment right to peacefully observe public actions of government officials, as well as his Fourth Amendment right to be free from illegal search and seizure.

Advertisement

It was the first time a Maine legal observer has sued ICE officers under the state’s civil rights act, according to Webbert. Peck added the U.S. government as a defendant as soon as he could.

“This is a national issue that we just happened to get on camera,” Webbert said.

Peck started recording the incident from his vehicle while parked on a side street off Route 1.

One of the officers told him that “what you’re doing is called impeding federal law enforcement,” and later said “if you continue to impede us and follow us, you will be arrested,” according to the suit.

An officer told Peck that he was violating a federal statute that makes it illegal to forcibly impede, resist or intimidate designated federal officers while they’re performing official duties. The suit alleges that following and observing a vehicle from a safe distance does not constitute interference and requests that the officers receive training to understand the scope of this statute.

“They’re just part of this culture that thinks they’re above the law,” Webbert said.

He thinks a precedent of legal accountability for law enforcement tactics could prevent instances of violence.

It’s fresh in Webbert’s mind, less than a month after Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was shot and killed in Biddeford by an ICE agent who was later identified as David Brouillette. Webbert said Peck, his client, wants to set a precedent to protect his immigrant neighbors.

The Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Justice, ICE and Andrew McCormack, a senior counsel with the U.S. Attorney’s Office did not immediately respond Monday to requests for comment about the suit.

text:
Amnesty International South Africa has urged government to immediately stop vigilante groups from targeting migrants and businesses, citing a rise in unlawful, violent actions.

Executive director Shenilla Mohamed warned that failure to take decisive action against a growing trend of vigilantism is encouraging further human rights violations. The organisation is demanding that police investigate and hold perpetrators accountable.

The crisis intensified ahead of a June 30 deadline issued by the group March and March, which ordered undocumented migrants to leave South Africa.

With the deadline passing, coordinated intimidation, harassment, and anti-migrant protests continue to disrupt communities, the organisation notes.

Mohamed emphasised that government statements are no longer enough to deter these groups.

“Authorities must move beyond statements of concern and demonstrate through effective investigations, prosecutions and accountability measures that no person or group is above the law,” she said.

Amnesty International cited the Immigration Act, which prohibits private citizens or groups from enforcing immigration laws.

This means private individuals cannot demand identity documents, enter private property, or evict people from homes and businesses and only designated immigration officers and members of the South African Police Service hold legal enforcement authority.

The organisation is calling for urgent interventions from State authorities, highlighting that allegations of police officers ignoring illegal acts or actively colluding with vigilante groups must face thorough criminal and disciplinary reviews.

The organisation wants the State to protect the right of business owners to operate safely without harassment, while upholding the right to dignity, freedom, and security for every person living in South Africa.

“Human dignity has no nationality and we cannot allow the unfettered violation of rights to continue,” Mohamed said.

She said where concerns exist about a person's immigration status, these must be addressed through lawful procedures that respect constitutional rights and human dignity.

“Even where individuals may be found to be undocumented, they remain entitled to rights protected under the Constitution and international human rights law, including due process, dignity and protection from violence and abuse,” she reminded.

Amnesty International South Africa and other civil society organisations have repeatedly warned that inflammatory rhetoric, anti-migrant mobilisation and weak State responses risk fuelling discrimination, violence and further human rights violations.

name: Human Rights
title: The Makings of a Mass Crisis | The Nation
authors: smccroskey, Dave Zirin, Kenia Akridge, Hannah Riley Fernandez, Laila Lalami, Stephen Zunes, The Nation, Mychal Denzel Smith, www.thenation.com
description:
What looked to be a massive humanitarian crisis was defused almost as soon as it had started.
That thousands of young Moroccans had spontaneously crossed into Ceuta after Spain’s Supreme Court ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not be sent back immediately.
Everyone was grasping for a sensible explanation to the crisis or some kind of strategy behind the madness.
Dignitaries in suits, jellabas, and caftans streamed into the palace for celebrations, while just a few miles away young Moroccans were throwing themselves into the sea hoping to cross into Spain.
In the last decade, we have witnessed many mass migration events: refugees fleeing Syria, Ukraine, Palestine, and Sudan, to name just a few.
text:
During the last week of July, as a heat wave desiccated the Mediterranean basin and wildfires ravaged cities on both sides of the sea, an estimated 50,000 Moroccan migrants crossed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in northern Morocco, swimming the short distance around the border post. By July 31, more than 48,300 had already returned home, after finding a local immigration processing center packed, shops and restaurants closed, and nothing to eat or drink. What looked to be a massive humanitarian crisis was defused almost as soon as it had started.

Theories quickly circulated on social media. That thousands of young Moroccans had spontaneously crossed into Ceuta after Spain’s Supreme Court ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not be sent back immediately. That Morocco had enabled these crossings after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited its political rival Algeria, to remind the prime minister that Morocco can still exert control over migration flows into Europe. That Morocco had sent people to the border at the behest of the United States and/or Israel, because the Sánchez government had recognized Palestine as a state. That Morocco wanted to reassert its territorial claims over Ceuta and Melilla, Spain’s last two outposts in Africa. Everyone was grasping for a sensible explanation to the crisis or some kind of strategy behind the madness.

The influx of migrants happened on Throne Day, when King Mohammed celebrated his 27 years in power at a series of ceremonies held in the north of Morocco. Dignitaries in suits, jellabas, and caftans streamed into the palace for celebrations, while just a few miles away young Moroccans were throwing themselves into the sea hoping to cross into Spain. The contrast was jarring. To add to the surreality, that evening the Moroccan Women’s National Team defeated its Algerian counterpart in the group stage of the Women’s African Cup of Nations, a qualifying event for the World Cup. Gianni Infantino, lately embroiled in a scandal over the privatization of FIFA, was present at the palace celebrations. You can’t write coincidences like this even in a work of fiction.

But it beggars belief that, in the week leading up to Throne Day, thousands of young people could stream to the border post unnoticed and unchallenged. Posts on social media had falsely claimed that anyone who made it to Ceuta by sea could obtain legal status in Europe. (In fact, residents in the Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla are subject to identity control and cannot freely enter Schengen Area countries.) Witnesses say that the Moroccan police enabled the crossings by pointing would-be migrants in the right direction. There are disturbing precedents. Back in July 2022, an estimated 2,000 sub-Saharan migrants scaled the fence into Ceuta, leading to a stampede in which two dozen were killed. And in May 2021, in the midst of a diplomatic row between Spain and Morocco over Western Sahara, more than 8,000 migrants were allowed to cross into Ceuta.

Spain and Morocco have a history that stretches back centuries. What happened at the border last week probably has more to do with internal politics and competing interests than with anything else. There may not be a simple or single reason, though there is a wider context. Relations between the two countries, which had warmed considerably after Sánchez announced his support for Morocco’s autonomy plan in Western Sahara, have been cooling again. Not long ago, the Spanish government said it would grant citizenship to people born during its colonial rule over the desert territory, a change in status it did not apply to its former colonial areas in northern Morocco. The decision likely came as a sign of bad faith in the autonomy plan that Morocco has long championed. But this, too, is conjecture. Until we know who started the online rumors promising legal status in Europe to people who cross by sea into Ceuta, we can’t say what triggered the migration event or why it wasn’t stopped in a week as sensitive as that leading to Throne Day.

Whatever the strategic (mis)calculations behind this crisis, what is indisputable is that on any given day, there are tens of thousands of young people in Morocco who are willing to risk everything for a chance to live in Europe. Men, women, and even families with young children took part. It didn’t seem to matter what studies reveal about the actual lives of undocumented people, or what newspapers report about low wages, social alienation, or human trafficking. The viral claims of legal status proved too tempting, and the images on social media too seductive.

Compounding the problem is the fact that, every summer, Moroccans from the diaspora return to the kingdom on holiday, spending their annual savings on cash and gifts for families back home, and providing a boost to the local tourist economy. Young Moroccans see friends and family members enjoying a lifestyle that they don’t have at home and conclude, not unreasonably, that Europe holds promises that their own country doesn’t.

What promises? Jobs, for one thing. The youth unemployment rate in Morocco is notoriously high, and, despite evidence to the contrary, many migrants believe they will find well-paying jobs in Europe. At least some of the people who joined the crowds crossing into Ceuta appear to be employed, if poorly, in their own country. A nurse told a Spanish news outlet that, for all his degrees and training, he makes €300 a month. These migrants want more than underemployment; they want decent wages and healthcare and a decent standard of living.

Rights, for another thing. Spain guarantees its people freedom of expression and bodily autonomy and a chance to live your life without interference from the government. Jobs and human rights together operate as “pull” factors, drawing the imagination of young Moroccans and making them believe that a better future means a future outside Morocco.

In the last decade, we have witnessed many mass migration events: refugees fleeing Syria, Ukraine, Palestine, and Sudan, to name just a few. People who escape civil war or genocide or starvation or atrocities of all kinds are determined, no matter what happens on their long and arduous journey, to make it to safety. But the Moroccan migrants who crossed into Ceuta did not appear to share this overwhelming desperation or unshakable determination. Nearly all of them returned just 24 hours after the crossing, which suggests they are not subject to a “push” factor.

Some expressed relief at being back in their homeland. A young woman who swam around the border post and found only a beach packed with other would-be migrants, a few corpses, and no resources of any kind, returned by land to Morocco and told a local news camera, “I ask forgiveness from all Moroccans.” A young man told a Spanish journalist, “To be honest, I don’t even know why I’ve come.” It was as if thousands of young Moroccans had been gripped by a mass delusion that they would be handed legal status and jobs, then quickly found out they were wrong. The grim result is that more than 70 people died in the crossing.

Morocco will be cohosting the World Cup with Spain and Portugal in 2030, and has embarked on vast infrastructure projects, including building newer stadiums, more railroads, and updated airport terminals. That thousands of Moroccans are willing to leave the country at the first sign of opportunity is a terrible indictment of these priorities. Unless the government provides better jobs, education, healthcare, and human rights to young people, the pull factors will remain, and the crisis we witnessed this last week will happen again.

text:
Maryland joined 24 Democrat-led jurisdictions that sued the Trump administration Monday to block a new policy that would allow a broad range of federal authorities to access personal information on families that receive Temporary Assistance for Needy Families payments.

In a separate suit Monday, Maryland was one of 25 jurisdictions to sue the administration over the imposition of what it called “unlawful” tariffs. They are just the latest in the dozens of legal actions against the federal government by Maryland and by the other states.

The TANF lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in the District of Columbia, claims a new Administration for Children and Families’(ACF) policy would let federal agencies access data on millions of residents who receive the assistance. The new policy is scheduled to go into effect Aug. 11 and would provide access to Social Security numbers, marital history, immigration status and more.

The program, which is under the federal Department of Health and Human Services, provides about $16 billion annually to states for low-income families.

Maryland receives about $228 million under the program, according to the office of Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown (D). In fiscal 2026, a monthly average of more than 38,000 participants (about 27,000 children and nearly 12,000 adults) were in the state.

“Families who rely on TANF to keep a roof over their children’s heads should not have to fear that their personal information will be shared across the federal government or used to target them,” Brown said in a statement. “My office will not stand by while this Administration unlawfully exposes Marylanders’ private data in an effort to intimidate vulnerable families out of benefits they are legally entitled to receive.”

Brown and the other attorneys general in the suit want the court to throw out the proposed rule and ensure the confidentiality of the personal information.

An ACF representative said in an email Monday evening that the agency doesn’t comment “on matters subject to ongoing litigation.”

Besides the agency, the lawsuit lists Assistant Secretary Alex J. Adams, the Office of Family Assistance and its director, David Swegle, and HHS and its secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as defendants.

The lawsuit claims a June 23 legal notice from HHS made the “extravagant” claim that ACF had authority to not only oversee the TANF programs in states, but to also share recipients’ data with other agencies to verify their “citizenship or immigration status in records maintained by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.”

The lawsuit claims that states, not the federal government, are in charge of verifying eligibility of applicants. It says the federal government’s policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Spending Clause of the Constitution by ignoring restrictions on data sharing in the low-income programs and enacting new, arbitrary conditions on federal funding.

According to the suit, the program’s recent use of its system of records could be used for three purposes:

To determine whether grantees are meeting certain requirements;

To compile information used in the report to Congress; and

To perform research on the caseload dynamics and employment trajectories of TANF recipients.

“Nothing in the TANF statute or any other act supports ACF’s extravagant claims of authority and gross breach of personal privacy,” the suit says. “There is no provision of the TANF statute that expressly authorizes ACF to enforce all provisions of the TANF statute against the States; indeed, the statute says precisely the opposite.”

Prosecutors drop vandalism charges for Reflecting Pool damage, blame ‘contractor error’

Besides Maryland and the District of Columbia, the other jurisdictions in Monday’s suit include the states of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin.

Those same states were part of the lawsuit against the Trump administration for imposing 10% and 12.5% tariffs last month on the European Union and 59 other countries that trade with the U.S.

The president imposed those tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 that’s used to combat “unfair trade practices” by other countries. The tariffs imposed in July affect over ​99% of U.S. ⁠imports.

The states’ lawsuit, which also includes North Carolina, was filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade in New York. It follows a May ruling that said the president’s 10% global tariff was unlawful. The 2-1 decision in that case also noted the president’s decision exceeded his authority.

But Trump has continued to pursue new tariffs, which he has made part of his foreign policy initiative since his second term in office.

“Every time a court strikes down these tariffs, this Administration comes back with a new scheme to impose unlawful costs on Maryland families,” Brown said. “My Office will not stand by while Marylanders are left footing the bill for groceries and everyday essentials because this Administration operates as if it is above the law.”

Brown’s office has led or joined in nearly three dozen legal actions this year against the Trump administration.

text:
A man from El Salvador has died at an immigration jail in New Jersey that has been the target of months of protests over living conditions for people detained there, federal officials said Monday.

Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, 41, had been held at Delaney Hall in Newark after being arrested June 18, according to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Lopez-Cornejo, whom the government accused of entering the U.S. illegally, died Saturday, the agency said. His official cause of death will be released following further medical examination, according to ICE.

Video above: Vetting of ICE officer involved in Biddeford shooting is under review, border czar says

Democratic politicians and civil rights groups in New Jersey questioned whether the death was preventable, saying they had little confidence people detained at the 1,000-bed facility were receiving proper care.

"This is not the first death of a detainee at Delaney Hall, and absent decisive action, it will not be the last," Democratic U.S. Sen. Cory Booker said in a statement. "I have visited the facility myself and witnessed these conditions firsthand, so I say this plainly: Delaney Hall must be closed immediately and permanently."

ICE said Lopez-Cornejo "received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals" while he was in custody.

The death is the second at Delaney Hall since the beginning of President Donald Trump's second term, according to tracking by The Associated Press. Another 41-year-old man, Jean Wilson Brutus, a Haitian national, died suddenly after collapsing in December in what a medical examiner ruled was a natural death due to a lung blockage.

In all, at least 56 people have died in ICE custody during Trump's second term. Lopez-Cornejo is the second native of El Salvador, following the September death of Norlan Guzman-Fuentes, who was killed during a sniper attack on an ICE field office in Dallas.

Video below: Judge orders ICE to release woman taken into custody after attending Noah Kahan concert

People held at the Newark facility have asked for improved living conditions and better medical care, as they say some are being denied medication. Earlier this year, some launched a hunger strike, according to Cosecha, an immigrant advocacy group.

The facility has also been a key flashpoint for protests against Trump's immigration crackdown, with demonstrators trying to block vehicles from entering or leaving the facility.

Trump and his deputies have defended the center's operations and denied there is any hunger strike, abuse or poor conditions inside.

The facility is owned by Geo Group, a private prison contractor that runs multiple detention centers across the country. The contractor did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, said her administration is working to better understand the facts surrounding his death.

"At the same time, we continue to face obstruction in our efforts to conduct a full health inspection of the facility," she said in a statement. "Every effort to block oversight raises serious questions about what is happening inside Delaney Hall and what those operating the facility are trying to hide."

Associated Press writer Ryan Foley in Iowa City, Iowa, contributed to this report.

text:
Migrant children incarcerated at a now-closed facility next to an Air Force Reserve base outside of Miami were exposed to toxic chemicals such as arsenic and lead, which are linked with developmental harm and cancer, according to more than 20,000 pages of records released as part of federal litigation over the site.

The Homestead migrant detention center for unaccompanied children, which closed in 2019, was situated adjacent to Homestead Air Reserve Base, a Superfund site, according to the social justice and environmental groups that sued in 2021 to make the documents public. The children, who were as young as six years old, also were subjected to the constant noise of F-16C fighter jets taking off and landing at the base, as well as sexual abuse, the groups said.

The litigation concluded last week after the federal government agreed to pay the groups’ legal fees. Earthjustice filed the lawsuit on behalf of the American Friends Service Committee in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, naming as defendants the Air Force, the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The Air Force declined to comment on the litigation. The other agencies did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Inside Climate News.

The situation fits a nationwide pattern of migrants incarcerated in harmful environments, said Guadalupe de la Cruz, Florida program director at the American Friends Service Committee. Some 60 miles northwest of the site, thousands of undocumented migrants were held in tents at the facility known as Alligator Alcatraz, which opened last year during hurricane season in a remote region of the Everglades. That facility closed this past June.

“It really does mark a victory of how much pressure organizations can be putting on the government for accountability,” said de la Cruz, of the Homestead site. “It really shows the repeated pattern, that the government has created facilities in areas that are not adequate to provide safe conditions for children or people to be in, and it’s become a common practice for the government to use contaminated land to set up detention facilities.”

The Obama administration opened the Homestead facility for children in 2016 as an “emergency influx shelter.” The Trump administration closed it briefly in 2017 but reopened it the next year, and its population swelled to more than 3,700 before the site closed amid public pressure, the groups said. The records the groups obtained showed some of the children detained at the facility were not unaccompanied minors but were taken from their parents at the U.S.-Mexico border. Despite the known history of contamination there, the documents revealed there was no evaluation for environmental hazards or remediation of the affected areas.

The site was near 16 sources of contamination, a concern in a coastal area vulnerable to intensifying hurricanes as the global climate warms. Hurricane Andrew destroyed much of the base in 1992, and a lack of a hurricane plan was another reason the detention facility closed. The contaminants are linked with developmental harm in children and can cause cancer and damage to the kidneys, liver and immune system. The fighter jet noise was at levels associated with cognitive injury and developmental harm. At one point the facility was the largest juvenile detention center in the country, the groups said.

“We need to be vigilant. We need to make sure, for kids but also for anybody, that the potential risks for health are being taken into account,” said Tania Galloni, managing attorney for the Florida regional office at Earthjustice. “We don’t think that happened here, and we don’t ever want to see that happen again.”

text:
OKLAHOMA CITY — U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin this weekend implored states and cities to cooperate with federal immigration officials, which he said would lead to safer and lower-profile arrests and deportations.

Speaking to a group of Democratic and Republican governors gathered for the National Governors Association summer meeting, Mullin called on local governments to help focus on removing the “worst of the worst” offenders, particularly targeting people without legal citizenship status who have criminal court convictions.

The Republican, who previously represented Oklahoma in the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House, took the stage with Oklahoma Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt, the outgoing chair of the national association. Mullin took over the agency after President Donald Trump fired former Secretary Krsti Noem, who defended the high-profile killings of American citizens by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

In his remarks on Saturday, Mullin asked states to cooperate with immigration detainers, in which the feds ask local governments to hold people in the country without legal authorization after they have served their time in prison or jail.

“That shouldn’t be controversial,” he said. “We’re not doing job-site raids. We’re not going to Home Depot and raiding the parking lot. These are individuals that have already been convicted of a crime.”

Trump administration claims court victory in mandatory detention

The secretary said the alternative for so-called sanctuary cities or states that don’t cooperate with ICE is a much more dangerous prospect: ICE agents pursuing arrests of people after they are released.

“We’re going to arrest them, and then we’re going to arrest them in a public space, which could cause more problems and put our officers at risk, the public at risk, and the person we’re serving the detainer at risk.”

Mullin highlighted the department’s recent success during the World Cup in cooperating with law enforcement, which he said not only ensured the safety of locals and visitors, but provided meaningful human trafficking prevention and the confiscation of counterfeit goods.

“We can’t do it without you guys,” he said. “I’m saying we can work together.”

He focused on cooperation in Oklahoma, where 76 of the state’s 77 counties are working with the federal government to remove immigrants before they are released from jails and prisons.

“It’s not on the news,” he said. “You don’t see us around because the state is doing most of the work.”

Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who took over leadership of the bipartisan governors group this week from Stitt, thanked the secretary for opening up lines of communication with states since taking over.

“There is an absolute difference in what we have seen from the start of the administration to now,” he said.

Moore questioned Mullin about the status of federal security grants, which can aid state anti-terrorism work, provide federal training and boost cybersecurity efforts.

Mullin said the first thing the agency looked at was whether the local government was cooperating with federal law enforcement.

“The whole point of the grants is so we can have partnerships,” he said. “…This has nothing to do with picking winners and losers or saying I choose Oklahoma over California — this has to do with it is designed by nature to build a partnership.”

At least 15 states, including Maryland, are identified as sanctuary states by the Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates for lower levels of immigration.

Undocumented immigration population reached as high as 15.8M, report finds

Mullin’s comments over the weekend sparked backlash from some Republicans, including prominent Trump ally Steve Bannon. Some of those pundits said Mullin was too lax on deportations after he acknowledged the legal steps migrants could take to gain legal status.

Mullin said naturalization ceremonies occur constantly with nearly 900,000 people becoming U.S. citizens in the past year.

But he said federal officials will have no tolerance for migrants with criminal convictions or those who have not taken the legal steps to remain in the country.

Under Mullin’s watch, ICE has made a record number of immigration arrests.

Immigration arrests reached 1,593 per day in early July in a new push to detain and deport immigrants. In June, there were more than 43,000 arrests, the highest recorded by the Trump administration, according to statistics from ICE.

“There’s a legal system to go through,” he said. “But if you choose not to even begin or not to change your status, if you’ve been here 25 years, I can’t help you.”
