title: Seeking Sanctuary in America | Civic News. Empowering Nonprofits. Advancing Justice.
authors: Julia Luz Betancourt, Dr. PennElys Droz, Candice Fortin, Darakshan Raja, Nikayla Jefferson, Peggy Shepard, Kyle T. Mays, Kailea Loften, Bitter Kalli
description:
In 2017, Cinthya Santos Briones witnessed up close what it took for immigrants to avoid deportation in Trump’s America.
For the majority-immigrant workers who anchor the U.S. plant nursery industry, abusive and exploitative working conditions have left them fighting for survival in a hotter, more hostile America.
But hidden behind the leaves and petals is a human rights crisis claiming the lives and health of immigrant workers in Florida.
At the same time, the state remains a focal point of the dangers of U.S. labor exploitation as climate change intensifies.
is working to transform those conditions by building a grassroots, bottom-up movement driven by immigrant workers.
text:
Nonprofit Quarterly (NPQ) has partnered with Counterstream Media to co-publish Peace & Riot’s latest issue—a collection of more than 20 voices exploring climate leadership on the frontlines, in communities, and in the culture. Read the full Peace & Riot issue here.

In 2017, Cinthya Santos Briones witnessed up close what it took for immigrants to avoid deportation in Trump’s America. During a presidency marked by a surge in infamously cruel ICE arrests, deportations, and family separations, she spent days escorting immigrants to court appointments and volunteering at legal clinics in different areas of the country.

Even before then, Santos Briones knew migrating to the United States could result in danger upon arrival. She and her family left Mexico to live in the U.S., where she watched her loved ones navigate life while undocumented. Yet, as an ethnohistorian, she was determined to document how others like them managed to survive. So when she wasn’t at the courts or clinics, she photographed the people who hid away in churches, temples, and faith spaces, learning to stay put in a country that tried relentlessly to send them away.

Living in Sanctuary, her photojournalism series, showcased immigrants who sought refuge in places of worship, which are not required to enforce immigration laws. Taken together, the photos illuminate some of the everyday actions these communities took in resistance to the first Trump administration’s ruthless immigration policies.

“Living there meant inhabiting a prolonged waiting: days marked by fear of a raid, but also by simple routines—cooking, praying, celebrating birthdays—that insisted on life as a political act,” Santos Briones wrote in a summary of the series. “In the face of intensified criminalization, faith-based movements persist—sometimes less visibly—sustaining their communities through accompaniment, protection, and discreet networks of care.”

Reflecting on the project almost a decade later, she tells me the photographs also challenge the romanticization of America as a sanctuary.

“Even though the idea of sanctuary sounds beautiful, [migrants] spent two years, one year, or four years inside of churches without going outside, because they were at risk of being deported or kidnapped by ICE,” she said. “At the same time that it was a sanctuary for them, it was more like a church arrest.”

“The words “give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free” remain etched on the Statue of Liberty. In reality, the so-called land of the free has disproportionately targeted non-white migrants for deportation throughout history. And now, it is shutting its borders to most refugees.

For centuries, the U.S. has considered itself a sanctuary for people of the world, promising them a chance at “the American dream.” The words “give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free” remain etched on the Statue of Liberty. In reality, the so-called land of the free has disproportionately targeted non-white migrants for deportation throughout history. And now, it is shutting its borders to most refugees.

The Supreme Court greenlit the end of Temporary Protected Status in June, leaving hundreds of thousands of Haitian and Syrian refugees fleeing war and natural disasters at risk of deportation. More broadly, people forced from home due to climate change face even tighter restrictions on gaining entry into the U.S.

These deliberate policy decisions are just the latest in a long line of racially exclusive immigration laws and codes. But while U.S. rules around citizenship and legal status are arbitrary, they are becoming more punitive, sentencing both people and the planet to a cycle of devastation.

Since the start of Trump’s second term, agencies have increased their use of AI technology to locate immigrants and store their personal data, driving up demand for data centers and the mining of Indigenous territories.

Natural river flows in the Rio Grande are under threat as the federal government constructs thousands of miles of industrial-grade buoys with the intent of making the river impossible to swim across. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is overcrowding detention centers, building new facilities on fragile ecosystems like Florida’s Everglades, and operating and reopening others in toxic areas.

As deportations surge, the climate consequences of expelling hundreds of thousands of people will inevitably be felt by communities far beyond the U.S. and its borders.

The U.S. was already one of the largest emitters of greenhouse gases before Trump’s second term. Then ICE administered more than 20,000 deportation flights between January 2025 and April 2026, spiking the agency’s carbon emissions by 88% from the year before and releasing an estimated 370,240 tons into the atmosphere.

But Santos Briones sees another side to the immigration story, one focused on community and healing rather than policing and pain. It’s a story that lives in their relationships to plants.

Healing by and for the People

“Healing plays a huge role in our society and in our community,” Santos Briones said. “Our plants have immigrated with us. Like epazote from Mexico. Like rosemary, or cilantro. They are not native to America, but they were brought through different periods of colonization.”

In 2019, Santos Briones created Herbolario Migrante, or Migrant Herbalism, a community workshop and traveling art series that circulates traditional knowledge of Afro-Indigenous herbal medicines from Latin America and the Caribbean around New York City.

The project’s purpose is to recover how herbs, plants, minerals, seeds, and barks are used for healing in displaced Indigenous immigrant communities. For a one-to-two-month period, immigrants share stories about the herbal remedies passed down in their families and record these remedies through photographs, textiles, poems, and more, preserving them in what Santos Briones calls a “collective archive.”

“When I suffered from eye problems, José Juarez, a Totonac healer and migrant, prescribed ritual objects designed to provide spiritual protection and promote healing. Among them were animal-shaped amulets, religious figures, spiritual soaps, herbal remedies, potions, and magical powders.” – Cinthya Santos Briones

“This is, for me, participatory ethnography—how I am going to research [and] include the voices of the community in my project. It’s not just about me, only. It’s also about what the people think,” she said. “In anthropology, we include their testimonies, even though we don’t call them collaborators. They are our subject. It’s really colonial vocabulary.”

The majority of participants at Santos Briones’s workshops are working-class, immigrant women. With her support, they learn embroidery and create cyanotypes (prints made by laying herbs on a piece of paper coated with solution before leaving it out in the sun, and without using a camera). By the end of the workshop, the group produces a catalog of plants that include written stories and recipes detailing their use, which is then exhibited at a local museum.

“We [immigrants] are not just a force in this country. We are not just our labor. We bring knowledge, and Migrant Herbalism speaks to that.”

“It’s important that the women see the result. It’s important to take them away from [their own] community and to other neighborhoods in the city, other spaces that they usually think are not for them,” said Santos Briones. “They need to reclaim these spaces, like museums and galleries, in a civic intervention.”

“We [immigrants] are not just a force in this country. We are not just our labor,” she added. “We bring knowledge, and Migrant Herbalism speaks to that.”

“In 2020, after dealing with a serious eye health problem for over a year, I was diagnosed with a chronic eye disease. For months I had blurry vision and constant pain in my eyes, my eyelids were swollen. It was the height of the pandemic and seeing a doctor was almost impossible. To heal my eyes I started using medicinal plants, doing cleansings with daturas, power plants. Don José Juárez, a healer friend —katsiná— an indigenous Totonac, gave me a tecomaxochitl plant (floripondio) to protect me spiritually. In his botanical garden he made me a series of lak-pakti (cleansings) with medicinal and divinatory herbs such as ololiuhqui. I saved these plants and with the flowers from the harvest of the daturas that he gave me I began to make images using the lumen technique to portray the soul and spirit of these plants. After a few months of placing the flowers of the tecomaxochitl on my eyes I began to heal.” – Cinthya Santos Briones

For Santos Briones, a descendant of the Nahua Tribe, preserving this cultural knowledge is personal. Her family left their small town of Pueblo in the 1980s and ‘90s for a chance at life in the U.S. She worked for ten years at the National Institute of Anthropology and History, researching in the region where her paternal family is from in La Huasteca, Mexico.

Studying in Indigenous communities as an anthropologist taught her about herbs, shamans, and other kinds of healers whose traditions live on in today’s immigrant generations—and whose care work provides a safety net as enforcement and healthcare barriers make life in the U.S. more precarious.

“Herbolario Migrante is a project where I investigate the diversity of medicinal herbs that have migrated in recent decades due to the forced displacement of diverse communities from Mexico and Abya Yala to the United States. I also reflect on how the use of herbs, traditional medicine, its healing practices and rituals have crossed borders and subsisted through time. Inspired by Anna Atkins’ photographs of seaweed, I created a series of cyanotypes on cotton fabric, made from the healing herbs that have migrated with us and that I have collected from Mexican grocery stores in New York City neighborhoods. Each cyanotype archives a variety of diverse components including barks, pollen, seeds, flowers, petals, leaves, and branches, which can appear alone or assembled in bouquets.” – Cinthya Santos Briones

“These are a lot of displaced Indigenous peoples who have a really strong relationship to Earth, plant medicine, and community care networks, and thrive in those community care settings.”

In Sonoma County, California, for example, a nonprofit mobile herb clinic known as the Botanical Bus is bringing culturally-centered, collaborative healthcare services to Latine and Indigenous immigrant communities. Aiming to radicalize the care system, the clinic runs four main programs: an apothecary, wellness workshops, Healing Harvest, and Promotoras. The programs are designed to meet people’s health needs with traditional ecological knowledge. They are guided by a team of Latine and Indigenous community health workers—all of whom are immigrants or the daughters of immigrants—who provide trusted, culturally relevant health services to their own community.

“These are a lot of displaced Indigenous peoples who have a really strong relationship to Earth, plant medicine, and community care networks, and thrive in those community care settings,” said Jocelyn Boreta, who co-founded the clinic in 2019. “That is where healing justice exists in these moments, because these care networks are thriving and people are feeling nourished, as if they belong to the Earth, wherever they choose to be.”

Boreta, a licensed herbalist who is of Nahua heritage and the granddaughter of an Indigenous farmworker, launched the organization alongside a group of Latine women to blend care and community organizing. The clinic’s fully-functioning herbal apothecary carries more than 100 dried herbs—including culturally appropriate herbs such as manzanilla and lemon balm—and is run by a lead clinical practitioner and a team of nine clinical apprentices, who each identify as Latine Indigenous herbalists and are in the process of developing their own culturally-centered clinical practices.

In 2025, the Botanical Bus served 1,314 people from cities throughout Sonoma, Marin, and Napa counties and provided 2,500 health services. But Boreta emphasized that while the Botanical Bus seeks to break barriers to healing (98% of clients in 2025 reported that they felt supported, connected, seen, heard, respected, and understood), its goal is not to completely replace primary care. Rather, it hopes to expand access to primary care and uproot deep injustices in the healthcare system.

“There’s a real health disparity in the Latine and Indigenous immigrant communities,” said Boreta. “There is healing justice in Latine and Indigenous immigrant people having the power to find their own path to healing. That path is about access and agency…and being able to overcome some of those barriers is a form of activism.”

According to research conducted by the Botanical Bus, one third of their clients screen positive for anxiety or depression, more than half live in households affected by type-2 diabetes, and 83% face barriers to accessing primary care, 70% of whom identify financial barriers as the reason why they delay or forgo treatment altogether.

“Some of the top areas are fear of costs, difficulty navigating the medical system, of care not being offered in their language, and not feeling like they belong to care systems or that they can find themselves within the care that is being recommended,” Boreta added.

The data mirrors the healthcare gaps seen nationally, where immigration status can overwhelmingly determine health outcomes. A 2025 study by KFF and the New York Times found that almost half of likely undocumented immigrant adults and one in five immigrant adults with legal status reported lacking insurance.

After Trump rescinded a Biden-era policy intended to prevent ICE agents from entering protected areas like hospitals, doctor’s offices, and community health clinics, accessing critical healthcare services is becoming more dangerous for immigrants, who can be at risk of detention and deportation for simply seeking out basic survival needs.

But the Botanical Bus is showing that it is possible for immigrant communities to take charge of their health—even as the immigration system works against them. The mobile apothecary regularly travels to vineyard worksites and family service centers to support both immigrant farmworkers and their communities.

A growing network of health providers including federally qualified health centers are working in collaboration with the clinic to create “care hubs” where immigrant communities can receive wraparound services such as herbalism, nutrition, massage, acupuncture, foot care, art therapy, mindfulness, community circles, and shared meals in addition to primary care.

“In a time where border regimes are dictating belonging, we get to go back to our relationships, to plant medicine, to food that we enjoy with our loved ones, and we get to reclaim that belonging.”

The Botanical Bus Wellness Workshops, available online and at family service centers, spread Indigenous knowledge of herbal medicine by exchanging remedies and recipes. Their program, Healing Harvest, works with local farmers to grow and source herbs and plants from nearby communities.

Boreta says these programs have the power to not only transcend brutal border regimes, but also to uplift the healing abilities that immigrant communities carry.

“Across cultures, food and plants have a really strong power to connect us to a sense of place, even somatically,” she said. “In a time where border regimes are dictating belonging, we get to go back to our relationships, to plant medicine, to food that we enjoy with our loved ones, and we get to reclaim that belonging.”

Planting With Dignity

But the relationships that immigrants can have with plants are not always healing. For the majority-immigrant workers who anchor the U.S. plant nursery industry, abusive and exploitative working conditions have left them fighting for survival in a hotter, more hostile America.

The U.S. plant nursery industry is a multi-billion dollar enterprise. It boomed during the COVID-19 pandemic when an increasing number of consumers sought to beautify their homes and improve their mental health while staying indoors. But hidden behind the leaves and petals is a human rights crisis claiming the lives and health of immigrant workers in Florida.

“There are largely low-wage immigrant workers doing the work in the unregulated U.S. South…for poverty wages, in dangerous working conditions, and being exposed to systemic labor abuses like sexual harassment, toxic pesticides, and extreme heat,” said Oscar Londoño, Co-Executive Director at WeCount!, a human rights organization led by and fighting for immigrant workers in Florida. “What people also don’t know is how important Florida is to that national store.”

Florida produces nearly 70% of the nation’s indoor foliage, making it the “national epicenter” of the industry, according to WeCount!’s report, The Human Cost of Houseplants. At the same time, the state remains a focal point of the dangers of U.S. labor exploitation as climate change intensifies. Florida leads the entire country in heat-related hospitalizations. Plant nursery workers, alongside construction workers and farmers, are on the frontlines of this deadly dilemma.

Of the plant nursery workers WeCount! surveyed for its report, 86% reported accidents or illness on the job, including from heat stress and pesticide exposure. More than one third reported having no access to water at work—and 62% of those who did receive water said it was too dirty and unsanitary to drink.

Londoño, who is the son of immigrant parents from Colombia and Honduras, ties the lack of labor protections for Florida’s immigrant plant nursery workers back to the South’s history of racial exclusion.

“It was agricultural workers in the 1930s who were excluded from core labor rights because they were Black workers, and because of the connection of agriculture to an entire regime backed by slavery,” said Londoño. “And so the labor force has changed. More migration has come in. Agriculture in the South is now primarily done by immigrant workers with irregular immigration statuses.”

Agricultural and domestic workers are excluded from the 1935 National Labor Relations Act, forcing them to do without the foundational labor protections many workers are able to enjoy today, such as the right to organize, form a union, and collectively bargain.

To fill the gaps, WeCount!’s 2021 ¡Que Calor! campaign was on the verge of making history in passing the first-ever comprehensive local heat standard that year. Industry groups lobbied to halt it—and in July of 2024, House Bill 433 went into effect, banning local governments from enforcing heat standards.

Londoño says the lobbying groups responsible for the block hold ties to big agriculture, big construction, and one of the largest producers of ornamental houseplants in the world, Costa Farms.

ICE arrests in Florida are also among the highest in the country since Trump’s return. As a result, immigrant workers who are organizing for better wages and working conditions in the state grapple with a heightened threat of deportation, detention, and harassment, in addition to rising heat.

But WeCount! is working to transform those conditions by building a grassroots, bottom-up movement driven by immigrant workers. On Feb. 14, 2026, the organization launched Planting Justice, a statewide campaign to unite the power of workers and consumers to change the way the houseplant business operates.

In many ways, Planting Justice was inspired by the Fair Food Program, organized by the Coalition of Immokalee Workers in 2011, which transformed labor conditions in the tomato industry. Following in the coalition’s footsteps, WeCount! is fighting for plant nursery workers to not only merely have a say in their working conditions, but also to develop the standards nurseries should adopt to keep workers safe and protected while on the job.

This labor organizing model is known as worker-driven social responsibility, a counter to corporate social responsibility, which Londoño says treats sustainability as a narrow obligation that doesn’t encompass the workers themselves.

“Oftentimes we hear the narrative of, ‘Who will do the work if there are no immigrants?’ We actually have to ask ourselves, ‘What was the work that we allowed immigrants to do?’”

“Worker-driven social responsibility says if we’re going to develop standards that are going to help transform labor and human rights within a company or within a supply chain, workers have to be the ones who develop the standards, educate other workers on those standards, and play a key role in enforcing those standards,” he said. “Oftentimes we hear the narrative of, ‘Who will do the work if there are no immigrants?’ We actually have to ask ourselves, ‘What was the work that we allowed immigrants to do?’”

As part of the campaign, WeCount! has developed a code of conduct alongside hundreds of plant nursery workers that provides a comprehensive list of the health and safety standards and fair wages workers are owed, such as an industry-wide heat illness prevention protocol, the right to paid time off, independent audits, and more.

The vision of the campaign is to win legally-binding agreements between WeCount! and the corporate retailers who dominate the plant nursery industry, like Lowe’s, Home Depot, IKEA, and Walmart—which do business with Costa Farms—among others. If companies agree to adopt the code of conduct, they are required to do business only with nurseries that are in compliance with the standards the workers created.

“Ultimately, while [nurseries] feel invincible in a state like Florida or in the U.S. South because of lack of political will, regulations, and labor laws, it’s these multi-billion dollar companies at the top that are their main customers,” Londoño said. “If millions of consumers say, ‘We want you to take action on the supply chain. We want you to guarantee to us that the plant we bought in your store is free of labor abuse and exploitation,’ companies at the top have to respond.”

Challenging corporate norms may sound unpromising, but the Fair Food Program is a testament to what workers can win when they act together. Today, 90% of Florida’s tomato fields are part of the program, and farms all along the East Coast, as well as in Nebraska, Colorado, Wisconsin, and Minnesota are participating.

“If we want more plants or more greenery, if we want better food and better vegetables, if we want skyscrapers and cities to be built, we have to care that the workers who are doing that have what they need to live safe and dignified lives.”

Londoño believes that, if Planting Justice is successful in Florida, it could lift up the standards for plant nursery workers nationwide, so that no nursery worker anywhere in the country experiences labor abuse or exploitation.

“If we want more plants or more greenery, if we want better food and better vegetables, if we want skyscrapers and cities to be built, we have to care that the workers who are doing that have what they need to live safe and dignified lives,” he said. “With the level of dignity to say, ‘You are a protagonist, not just in defining what the problem is, but in shaping and fighting for the solution.’”

As the U.S. moves through what may turn out to be its hottest summer on record, the season of America’s 250th is waning. The White House’s own July 4 celebrations were delayed due to extreme heat, and a massive smoke cloud is rummaging through the U.S. at the time of this writing. It is a stark reminder that climate change has no borders.

And while the Trump administration may go to extremes to police its own people, it is stories like Santos Briones’s, Boreta’s, and Londoño’s that reveal the truth about this nation’s immigrant communities. The fight for their lives is a fight for the planet.

text:
74

(OSV News) — The Diocese of El Paso has shut down its long-running legal aid ministry to unaccompanied child migrants, as the Trump administration withholds almost $1 million in funding for work already performed.

Estrella del Paso announced July 31 that it had closed its Unaccompanied Children’s Program and laid off 13 employees, after its federal contract was not extended.

That non-renewal comes as the organization is still owed for work it has completed for the federal government, with no payments received since December 2025.

Heartbreaking update

In an Aug. 1 video statement posted to the organization’s Instagram account, executive director Melissa Lopez — who in July had warned Estrella’s reserves had been “completely depleted” by the federal government’s non-payment — described the news as a “heartbreaking update.”

“Without payment from the federal government, we simply can’t operate this program,” she said.

Lopez stressed that “unaccompanied children have a right to legal services and representation under U.S. law,” noting that “the federal government agreed to this contract and is now refusing to pay what they owe.”

According to its press release, the nonprofit is currently representing 243 unaccompanied migrant children.

Outlook for the children

“Our attorneys have an ethical and legal obligation to continue representing the children, despite the government withholding payment for these services,” said Estrella del Paso in its press release.

But Lopez told local media days ahead of the announcement that she and her team had “no understanding of what’s going to happen to those children come next week.

“We don’t know if they’re going to have legal representation,” she said. “The government as of yet has not identified who will take over this representation.”

In its press release, Estrella del Paso said that many of the children it aids “are survivors of trafficking, violence, and persecution,” and that they “have a legal right to legal services and legal representation under U.S. law.”

Without access to attorneys, said the organization, “children win the right to stay less than 1% of the time.”

In its July 31 announcement, Estrella del Paso said the Trump administration at present owes “nearly $1 million for services that have already been provided,” an amount set to “increase after invoices are submitted for work completed during the month of July.”

The William Wilberforce Trafficking Victim Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 reaffirmed that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has oversight of unaccompanied migrant children.

Under the act (which has further specifications for children from contiguous nations), the agency is required to provide unaccompanied children in HHS care with legal counsel, “to the greatest extent practicable and consistent with” the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Funding battle

Estrella del Paso and several counterpart organizations filed suit against HHS in March 2025, after the Trump administration moved to slash funding for such legal representation altogether.

While the cuts were blocked by a federal judge, the administration stopped payments after December 2025, and began requiring previously unrequested forms of work documentation, including privileged communications, as the basis for any future payment — a stipulation described by Estrella del Paso as a demand for “confidential information” to which the federal government “has no legal right.”

In its suit, Estrella del Paso and its fellow plaintiffs said the administration’s “unlawful cancellation of funding for legal representations” violated both the TVPRA and a 2024 foundational rule implemented by HHS’ Office of Refugee Resettlement.

The ORR rule requires the federal government to fund legal service providers for unaccompanied children if “available appropriations” exist, while ensuring children receive access to legal counsel.

Estrella del Paso said it is “among nearly 100 legal groups across the country that provide services to roughly 20,000 children under a federal contract,” with program funds appropriated by Congress for nearly two decades.”

The total now owed to those organizations for legal such counsel is approximately $65 million, said Estrella del Paso in its July 31 press release.

The court case remains ongoing, with proceedings set to continue in August.

In comments emailed to OSV News, the Office for Refugee Resettlement said it “remains fully compliant with legal and regulatory obligations and does not act in any way that could dissuade a child from seeking appropriate legal relief.”

ORR said that “the current bridge contract with Acacia Center for Justice” — the nonprofit managing the network of legal service organizations, including Estrella del Paso, that provided counsel to unaccompanied migrant children — “ended on July 31, 2026.”

“ORR offered Acacia the opportunity to receive a second bridge based on requirements that include they provide the data on who they represent and that they bill us when they submit applications for immigration relief,” said the federal agency in its email. “Acacia refused to accept this bridge.”

Vulnerable children

Lopez said in the July 31 press release that the issue “is not about paperwork or even non-payment of the bills this administration owes,” but rather “about more than 20,000 vulnerable immigrant children who deserve to have someone in their corner and the federal government’s choice to leave them to face the immigration system alone.”

“We know what happens to children that go to court without an attorney. In one word, it is deportation,” said Lopez.

Gina Christian is a multimedia reporter for OSV News. Follow her on X @GinaJesseReina.

text:
Agricultural workers harvest onions in a California field in this Library of Congress photo. Immigrants in the state face a dual threat from cuts to federal Medicaid and state Medi-Cal health coverage, as well as federal enforcement actions and deportation threats for undocumented immigrants. Photo: Carol M. Highsmith Archive, Library of Congress.

A new survey by the UFW Foundation found that undocumented farm workers across the United States report widespread concerns about immigration enforcement, with nearly nine in 10 respondents expressing fear of detention or deportation.

The findings, released Thursday during a briefing at the Los Angeles County Federation of Labor, are based on responses from 2,250 farm workers surveyed last year, according to the UFW Foundation.

The nonprofit said the report, “Under the Sun and Out of the Shadows”, is the first in-depth survey focused on undocumented agricultural workers’ experiences during increased immigration enforcement under the Trump administration.

Survey findings

According to the report, 92% of respondents said immigration raids and deportations have affected their employment. The survey also found that:

88% worry about detention or deportation.

90% fear family separation.

61% said they have reduced shopping because of immigration concerns.

29% reported avoiding medical care.

80% have lived in the United States for more than 10 years.

More than 40% have worked in agriculture for more than two decades.

The UFW Foundation said respondents came primarily from California, with additional participants from Washington, Michigan, Georgia and 12 other states.

The organization said surveying undocumented workers is challenging because many fear interacting with researchers. The nonprofit said it was able to conduct the survey by drawing from its farm worker database developed through its immigration legal services and community outreach programs.

Central Valley impact

Agriculture depends heavily on immigrant labor, making immigration enforcement a significant issue for growers, workers and rural communities throughout California’s Central Valley.

The survey also found that 76% of respondents support protections from detention and deportation, while 53% said they hope for a pathway to legal status and eventual U.S. citizenship. More than one-third said they want to participate more fully in their children’s school activities.

UFW Foundation CEO Erica Lomeli Corcoran said the organization hopes the findings help policymakers better understand the experiences of undocumented farm workers.

Jonathan Angulo, the UFW Foundation’s research and policy analyst fellow and an adjunct lecturer at San Diego State University Imperial Valley, said the survey demonstrates that many undocumented farm workers continue to seek meaningful immigration reform despite concerns about arrest, deportation and family separation.

The UFW Foundation said the report is intended to inform policymakers and the public as debates over immigration enforcement and agricultural labor continue.

text:
The Trump administration’s plan to deport more than 300,000 Haitians who just lost their lawful status after a Supreme Court ruling is showing a split screen in U.S. politics, with some Republicans openly rejoicing in the pending removals while others plead for leniency.

The high court’s June ruling ended temporary protected status (TPS) for both Haitians and Syrians, determining that courts don’t have the power to review the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) decision to scrap the status.

The ruling will have very real consequences for the more than 330,000 Haitian TPS holders, who starting Monday may see their status lapse and be at risk of deportation to a country that is dominated by rival gangs and has not had a stable government since its leader was assassinated in 2021.

“Happy National Haitian Removal Week to all who celebrate!” Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) wrote last Monday, the day the Supreme Court’s ruling took effect.

James Percival, the top lawyer at the DHS, quoted Semisonic’s 1998 hit in highlighting the ruling.

“When we won the TPS cases in the Supreme Court, we were clear. ‘It’s closing time. You don’t have to go home, but you can’t stay here,’” the attorney wrote last week.

And the department itself fashioned a graphic telling Haitians their “free trial of America has ended.”

For Haitians and Democrats in Congress, the mood is far less celebratory.

“The Trump administration is trampling over what had been a bipartisan consensus in the Congress when we first launched the TPS program decades ago, and of course the purpose of this program was to make sure that people who are here in the United States, where their original countries of origin are have been turned into places of great danger, that we don’t force people back into danger,” Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) said in a call with reporters Monday.

“We don’t force people back into situations where their lives and their livelihoods are threatened,” he added, calling the move “unconscionable.”

The administration likes to argue that temporary must mean temporary.

“Temporary protected status. Let me put the emphasis on that first word — temporary,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a video in which he encouraged Haitians to self-deport, including by trying to find other countries that will accept them, though it’s unclear which ones might.

“If you think you’re going to just wait out the Trump administration, it’s not going to work.”

But advocates for the program inside and outside of Congress say the protections are designed to respond to temporary conditions — and must be extended if the situation on the ground does not change.

“Community members, business owners, and families — all are now at risk of deportation back to a county deemed ‘too dangerous to visit’ by the U.S. government. The ending of this program is cruel and baseless; TPS protection must be reinstated,” Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) wrote on social platform X last week.

In many ways, Haiti’s designation is a textbook use of the TPS program, which can be activated for both natural disaster and political unrest.

It was first designated for TPS in 2010 in the wake of a 7.0 magnitude earthquake that is estimated to have killed 200,000 to 300,000 people. The country did not swiftly rebound from the devastation.

Then, in 2021, Haitian President Jovenel Moïse was assassinated, another episode from which the country has not yet recovered.

The State Department lists Haiti as a Level 4 Do Not Travel country, noting that it has been under a state of emergency since 2024, and the department withdrew all of its nonemergency personnel in 2023.

The nation has failed to organize new elections, and, as of 2024, the United Nations determined gangs control about 85 percent of the capital city Port au Prince.

Nonetheless, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has indicated it plans to quickly begin deporting Haitians in the country.

Guerline Jozef, founder and executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said her group has already been contacted by 50 Haitians living in Springfield, Ohio, who were told to report to the ICE office and then were outfitted with ankle monitors.

“What we are seeing within communities across the country is that ICE is changing the tactics because people are watching what’s going on,” Jozef told reporters.

“So, instead of them heavily descending on communities, they are using tactics to bring the people into their offices to either detain them or fit them with an ankle monitor and telling them that if they don’t self-deport, they will be called back to report within a month.”

To be sure, the future facing Haitians is one that divides the GOP.

Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) was a co-sponsor of a measure that passed the House with Republican support that would have extended TPS for Haiti for another 18 months but has failed to be taken up in the Senate given GOP objections.

Several GOP members from south Florida, which has a sizable Haitian population, had also been among those calling on President Trump to extend work permits for TPS holders and hold off on deportations, noting how many of those affected work in healthcare and in nursing homes.

“Many of the few of us that did vote for the TPS extension have indicated that we’re concerned about employers in our district,” Rep. Nicole Malliotakis (R-N.Y.) said last month, warning that agriculture, healthcare and hospitality businesses will lose workers.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) lamented that many in his state were now bracing for removal, including in the community in Springfield, the small Ohio city where Trump joined those voicing a baseless conspiracy theory that Haitians were eating people’s pets.

“The argument always is made that the situation in Haiti is better. Anyone who knows anything about Haiti or follows it knows that that simply is not true. Haiti is hell today, so you’d be sending people back, literally back to hell,” DeWine told CBS News, noting that the U.S. bars commercial flights into Port au Prince.

“The reason you can’t fly in there is because the gangs shoot at the planes, so no one can even fly in there. The situation is really horrible. This is a dysfunctional government — dysfunctional police. This is a country that’s in virtual chaos.”

He also credited Haitians for helping revive the struggling city of Springfield.

“It’s a mistake. It’s not good for the United States, and it’s not good for the state of Ohio. These are people who have helped Springfield really come back,. … The Haitians who are living there and employed there, they came there to work, and they came there because there were jobs that were not being filled by other people,” he said.

Two efforts that would have helped Haitians were blocked by one senator: Eric Schmitt, a Republican from Missouri.

Democrats tried to bring up both the House bill to extend TPS for Haitians, as well as another measure from Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) that would have given a pathway to U.S. citizenship to TPS holders from all 17 countries that have the designation.

In both cases, Democrats attempted to bring the legislation to the floor under unanimous consent, a process that can be blocked with an objection by a single lawmaker.

Schmitt has boasted in recent days of blocking the pair of bills.

“Democrats asked the Senate to extend Haitian ‘temporary’ protected status,” he said on the Senate floor while miming air quotes.

“Today, they dropped the quotation marks. … Today, Democrats finally admit what this scheme was always designed to be: Temporary was always meant to be permanent. It’s the final stage of the scam, but that’s how Democrats do mass amnesty. First, they declare an emergency, then they import hundreds of thousands of people. They then extend the program over and over and over,” Schmitt said of the Haiti TPS bill.

He similarly objected to the legislation that would have allowed TPS holders to seek citizenship.

“America is a nation, not a global waiting room, not a refugee camp, not a lifetime stay at a taxpayer-funded hotel. Our immigration laws exist to serve the American people,” he said.

“Foreign nationals do not have a right to permanent settlement here.”

text:
A federal judge has struck down a New York law prohibiting federal officers from wearing masks, a setback for the state’s efforts to stop a notorious aspect of the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement campaign.

The Constitution’s Supremacy Clause does not allow New York to regulate federal law enforcement activities, District Judge Mae A. D’Agostino said in a ruling Monday.

“New York cannot impose its own uniform requirements on federal agents simply because it disagrees with how the Federal Government is exercising its authority,” D’Agostino wrote.

D’Agostino , an Obama appointee, upheld a New York law that bans local and state law enforcement authorities from cooperating with the Department of Homeland Security through what are known as 287(g) agreements, writing that the state has the authority to regulate its own police agencies.

The decision is a victory for the Trump administration, which has successfully challenged similar laws attempting to force Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to stop wearing masks and display their badges while making arrests.

A federal judge blocked a similar mask ban in California, and the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals went on to block the state’s law requiring federal officers to wear visible badge numbers and names. The administration has also challenged similar laws in Connecticut, New Jersey, Virginia and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

The administration has argued that forcing ICE agents to uncover their faces would expose them to harassment and doxxing, while detractors contend that such laws are necessary to hold federal agents accountable and to mitigate public fear.

“As reaffirmed by a federal court in New York, laws banning federal agents from wearing protective masks are unconstitutional,” Kiersten Pels , a DOJ spokesperson, said in a statement. “This Department of Justice is focused on law and order, public safety, and will not tolerate any violence directed toward law enforcement officials working tirelessly to keep Americans safe.”

State Attorney General Letitia James and Gov. Kathy Hochul said in a joint statement that their offices “are reviewing all legal options at this time,” and that “we stand firm in our belief that masked agents do not make New York safer.”

State lawmakers in Albany passed the mask ban in May, alongside other laws meant to regulate ICE officers amid the Trump administration’s increase in immigration enforcement. The federal government sued New York in late June, a week before the ban was set to go into effect.

The ruling, D’Agostino wrote, does not weigh in on the morality of immigration enforcement or whether the federal government has conducted its business in a sufficiently transparent manner, instead focusing on the constitutional question of whether New York’s laws attempted to regulate a federal agency.

“Defendants’ perspective is grounded in unavoidable observations of recent troubling events which loom darkly over the public perception of the manner in which federal immigration law is enforced,” D’Agostino wrote. “New York appears to be well-intentioned in its pursuit of transparent policing.”

title: Malaysia: Forcibly Returning Myanmar Refugees Risks Lives | Human Rights Watch
description:
“Malaysia has for many years hosted refugees from Myanmar who have fled unending oppression and atrocities by the Myanmar military,” said Bryony Lau, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
More than 215,000 refugees and asylum seekers are registered with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Malaysia, about 194,000 of them from Myanmar, including 126,000 ethnic Rohingya.
Malaysian authorities strictly enforce immigration laws and do not distinguish among refugees, asylum seekers, trafficking victims, and undocumented migrants in conducting raids.
Rohingya, as the largest ethnic group from Myanmar in Malaysia, have been the focus of public anger toward refugees.
In late May, an online petition calling for the removal of Rohingya refugees, accompanied by a disinformation campaign, caused an escalation in hate speech and vigilante violence targeting Rohingya.
text:
(Bangkok) – The Malaysian government should reverse plans that would permit the forced return of refugees to Myanmar, where they face persecution and other rights abuses, Human Rights Watch said today.

On July 23, 2026, Malaysia’s deputy foreign minister informed parliament that 5,000 Myanmar nationals in immigration detention would be sent back to Myanmar. On July 29, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said that Myanmar authorities had agreed to take back 5,000 ethnic Rohingya.

“Malaysia has for many years hosted refugees from Myanmar who have fled unending oppression and atrocities by the Myanmar military,” said Bryony Lau, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Malaysian government should show regional leadership in responding to the crisis in Myanmar rather than forcibly returning people who are the targets of the junta’s brutality.”

There are no authoritative figures on the number of Myanmar migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers in Malaysia. More than 215,000 refugees and asylum seekers are registered with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Malaysia, about 194,000 of them from Myanmar, including 126,000 ethnic Rohingya. For decades, UNHCR has processed asylum requests in Malaysia and provided successful applicants with cards recognizing them as refugees, but the cards do not grant legal status.

Recent announcements by Malaysian officials about UNHCR’s role and plans to send people back to Myanmar come amid surging immigration raids and xenophobic rhetoric that have fostered intense public hostility toward refugees and mistrust of UNHCR.

Malaysia has long lacked a legal framework for determining refugee status and all irregular entry and stay in the country is a criminal offense. Malaysian authorities strictly enforce immigration laws and do not distinguish among refugees, asylum seekers, trafficking victims, and undocumented migrants in conducting raids.

As of June 30, 22,166 people were in Malaysia’s immigration detention centers, about half of them from Myanmar, according to statistics provided by the home minister to Parliament.

On July 30, the home minister said that preparations were already underway to identify individuals who could be sent back through a new process to issue a Refugee Registration Document (Dokuman Pendaftaran Pelarian, or DPP), Malaysia’s new system for assessing asylum claims and registering refugees.

The government initiated the DPP system in January to take over responsibility for refugee registration from UNHCR and to improve oversight and minimize fake documentation. Refugees registered through the new system will be allowed to stay in Malaysia temporarily and will have the right to work, according to the terms of an unpublished directive by the National Security Council, known as MKN 23.

As of early July, Malaysian authorities had processed 128 Rohingya held in immigration detention through the DPP system, according to the home minister. Of those, 78 had been determined to be refugees, of whom 25 would be eligible to work. The minister did not explain what would happen to Rohingya who had not been granted refugee status.

Malaysian authorities have not indicated whether the system will comply with basic standards for refugee status determination, such as nondiscrimination, criteria grounded in international law, procedural integrity, strict confidentiality, data protection, and access to appeal, Human Rights Watch said.

As part of the rollout of the new system, the Malaysian government told UNHCR in July to temporarily stop registering refugees. The change further curtails UNHCR’s activities in Malaysia. Since 2019, the Malaysian government has denied UNHCR access to immigration detention centers, preventing the agency from reviewing asylum claims or assisting detainees who are registered refugees.

While Malaysia has not ratified the 1951 UN Refugee Convention or its 1967 protocol, it is still obligated to respect the international law principle of nonrefoulement, which prohibits countries from returning anyone to a place where they would face a real risk of persecution, torture or other serious ill-treatment, a threat to life, or other comparable serious human rights violations.

Since the February 2021 military coup in Myanmar, Malaysia has summarily deported thousands of asylum seekers to Myanmar without assessing their asylum claims or other protection needs and in violation of a Malaysian court order. In May 2024, UNHCR issued guidance stating that people fleeing Myanmar “are likely in need of international refugee protection.”

Conditions for safe, dignified, and voluntary return to Myanmar do not currently exist, Human Rights Watch said. The Myanmar military continues to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity. Junta authorities have arbitrarily arrested tens of thousands of people since the coup and thousands have died in custody.

Rohingya, as the largest ethnic group from Myanmar in Malaysia, have been the focus of public anger toward refugees. In late May, an online petition calling for the removal of Rohingya refugees, accompanied by a disinformation campaign, caused an escalation in hate speech and vigilante violence targeting Rohingya.

Rohingya have fled Myanmar to escape successive waves of atrocities against them by the Myanmar military. These atrocities include acts of genocide in 2017, the crime against humanity of apartheid, and more recent war crimes and other abuses by the ethnic Rakhine armed group, the Arakan Army, which has been fighting the Myanmar military for control of Rakhine State since late 2023. Myanmar’s denial of citizenship to Rohingya has left them especially vulnerable to human rights violations.

“The Malaysian government is fueling hostility towards refugees when it should be building support for and trust in its new refugee registration system,” Lau said. “People fleeing Myanmar have come to Malaysia seeking protection and should be able to stay while their asylum claims are fairly assessed, without living in fear of harassment, arrest, and forced return.”

description:

text:
BALTIMORE — Today, the District Court of Maryland temporarily blocked a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) rule that prevented nonpartisan civic engagement groups from registering new U.S. citizens to vote at administrative naturalization ceremonies. The Court’s preliminary injunction prevents the new rule from going into effect while the case is litigated.

The rule — which was issued abruptly in August 2025 and without factual basis — silenced the voices of Americans, but has been temporarily blocked following a lawsuit filed by Campaign Legal Center on behalf of the League of Women Voters (LWV) and a number of state and local Leagues. Now, civic engagement groups can continue the important work of educating and registering new Americans at administrative naturalization ceremonies — a longstanding tradition that encourages participation in the political process.

“When people become American citizens, they should be welcomed into full participation in civic life, not met with new barriers,” said Celina Stewart, CEO of the League of Women Voters. “For generations, the League has stood beside new citizens as they take the oath of citizenship and prepare to make their voices heard at the ballot box. Today’s ruling protects that fundamental democratic principle, and we will continue fighting to ensure every eligible voter can participate freely and fully in our democracy.”

“Any attempt to limit the freedom to vote is an attempt to silence American voters. This victory protects naturalized citizens’ access to the ballot box and the constitutional rights of civic organizations that help new citizens exercise their democratic freedoms,” said Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at the nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center. “We’ll continue to fight in court to make this victory permanent and protect naturalized citizens and the groups that help welcome them into our democracy.”

To read quotes from the individual state and local League plaintiffs, click here.

The plaintiffs sued the administration for violating the First Amendment rights of the national League of Women Voters and state and local Leagues to engage in political speech and associational activities. The suit also addresses the administration’s failure to obey the Administrative Procedure Act that requires federal agencies to follow clearly defined and transparent procedures when adopting new policies.

The League of Women Voters is a nonpartisan, grassroots, membership-based civic engagement group that has long exercised its constitutionally protected right to educate and assist new Americans in registering to vote at administrative naturalization ceremonies. Over the past few decades, the League has registered hundreds of thousands of new U.S. citizens to vote after naturalization ceremonies nationwide. No organization has done more voter registration at naturalization ceremonies than the League of Women Voters. Indeed, in 2024, the League registered more than 15% of all new American citizens to vote at naturalization ceremonies.

As a result of USCIS’s rule change, however, state and local Leagues were forced to cancel hundreds of planned voter registration events, where League members and volunteers expected to register thousands of new voters. Since USCIS’s unlawful rule has been in place, state and local Leagues have been prohibited from attending and assisting new citizens in registering to vote for more than eight months. But, with this Court victory, the League can now restart its important work with new citizens at administrative naturalization ceremonies.

Follow the latest updates on this lawsuit via CLC’s case page or the League’s legal center.

###

The nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center advances democracy through law. We safeguard the freedom to vote, defend voters’ right to know who is spending money to influence elections, and work to ensure public trust in our elected officials.

Aug. 3 (UPI) -- A coalition of 24 Democratic states on Monday sued the Trump administration to prevent immigration authorities from accessing private data from millions of families receiving anti-poverty aid.

Administration officials in June sent a notice to states expanding federal oversight of the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program.

The notice would allow the Administration for Children and Families to share detailed personal information from benefit recipients with other federal agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security.

"The Trump Administration has tried time and again to weaponize every aspect of government as part of their reckless immigration enforcement efforts," New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said in a statement.

"Now, they want to misuse a program intended to help vulnerable families and children as a tool for harassing immigrants," added Davenport, who joined the lawsuit. "Federal law sets clear limits on the sharing of sensitive personal data, but the administration would obliterate those guardrails and violate the privacy of families that are just trying to make ends meet."

Congress created TANF in 1996 to provide states with funding to provide assistance to low-income families with children.

The program provides $16 billion to states and tribal governments, which in turn administer the funds.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the federal effort is "cruel, unnecessary and illegal."

"While the Trump Administration continues to break the law in order to amass an ever-greater trove of people's personal information, we'll continue stepping in to protect the privacy of our people," Bonta said in a statement. "You have my word."

The Trump administration has repeatedly tried to access data from welfare recipients to share with immigration agents, Politico reported.

Federal officials say the efforts are necessary to prevent undocumented immigrants from receiving such benefits, for which they are not eligible.

text:
NEWARK — Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, a 41-year-old illegal alien from El Salvador who was detained at Delaney Hall Detention Facility, was pronounced deceased Aug. 1 by medical personnel at University Hospital in Newark, New Jersey.

When Lopez-Cornejo experienced a medical emergency while in ICE custody, GEO facility staff and medical staff responded immediately and called 911 for emergency medical services. The official cause of death remains pending further medical examination.

U.S Border Patrol arrested Lopez-Cornejo for illegally entering the United States without inspection on or about Aug. 13, 2006. On August 25, 2006, a DOJ immigration judge ordered him removed, and Lopez-Cornejo was removed to El Salvador on October 19, 2006. He illegally reentered the U.S. at a later unknown date. On June 18, 2026, ICE arrested Lopez-Cornejo in Plainfield, New Jersey. He was subsequently detained at Delaney Hall Detention Facility pending removal from the United States pursuant to a reinstatement of his prior removal order.

While in custody, Lopez-Cornejo received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.

Consistent with ICE policy, Enforcement and Removal Operations notified the Department of Homeland Security, the ICE Office of Inspector General and the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility via the Joint Intake Operation Center. The Consulate of El Salvador in Elizabeth, New Jersey, as well as Lopez-Cornejo’s next of kin, were also notified.

ICE makes official notifications to Congress, nongovernmental organization stakeholders and the media upon reports of in-custody deaths and posts news releases with relevant details on its public website. Information is available in the ICE Newsroom and on the Detainee Death Reporting page.

ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay. All people in ICE custody receive medical, dental and mental health intake screenings within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arriving at a facility, access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care. At no time during detention is a detained noncitizen denied emergency care.

text:
The Trump administration’s demand for states to provide Social Security numbers, immigration status, and other private information on low-income residents who receive cash benefits is improper and unconstitutional, a group of mostly Democratic-led states alleges in a new lawsuit.

Officials with 24 states and the District of Columbia say in the complaint that a regulatory change proposed by the U.S. Administration for Children and Families and set to take effect Aug. 11 greatly exceeds the federal government’s assigned role in overseeing the antipoverty program called TANF, or Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, and violates multiple privacy laws.

The change, first announced in June, will also cost states extra time and money and chill participation in a program that benefits some 2.4 million people nationwide, according to the 60-page lawsuit filed Monday in federal court in D.C. The states are calling for the court to throw out the proposed rule and ensure the confidentiality of this information.

New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport said in a statement that the regulatory change would “obliterate” existing guardrails on sensitive data and “violate the privacy of families that are just trying to make ends meet.”

“The Trump Administration has tried time and again to weaponize every aspect of government as part of their reckless immigration enforcement efforts. Now, they want to misuse a program intended to help vulnerable families and children as a tool for harassing immigrants,” Davenport said.

States have the right to “protect critically needed services for families in their time of greatest need,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in a statement.

“Families turn to these programs because they’re doing everything they can to keep a roof over their heads and food on the table — these programs are a literal lifeline for struggling parents and their kids,” Rayfield said. “But the Trump Administration is trying to weaponize these emergency assistance programs, taking families’ private, personal data and using it to advance a partisan political agenda that is tearing communities apart.”

The lawsuit alleges the change is part of the Trump administration’s ongoing effort to target immigrants by tightening the rules around various social service programs. Administration officials say they are trying to root out fraud and abuse, but critics say the new rules are designed to force out people who were born outside the U.S.

The Administration for Children and Families did not respond to a request for comment on Monday. According to the lawsuit, the administration said it will share the data it obtains with other government agencies or private entities as part of its quest to verify that states are properly spending taxpayer dollars.

Nothing in the law supports the federal department’s “extravagant claims of authority and gross breach of personal privacy,” the lawsuit says.

“The sharing of such information runs afoul of a thicket of federal privacy protections,” it says.

When TANF was created as part of a federal welfare overhaul in 1996, it was purposely designed to limit the federal government’s role and give states wide control over the program’s design, operation, and information verification, according to the lawsuit. The Trump administration has insisted problems with the program require greater federal scrutiny.

The regulatory change announced in June would force states to provide additional details on participants, including Social Security numbers, country of origin, and immigration status, even though 95% of children and 85% of adults receiving benefits are U.S. citizens, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit also alleges that the Trump administration has not specified how they plan to keep program participants’ data safe, that the change would place a “direct and significant” cost on states, and that releasing data to the federal government would erode trust state agencies have developed with participants.

The plaintiffs are New York, D.C., California, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin.

text:
David Venturella, the acting director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), sent a letter to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) saying he has divested of his Geo Group stocks and “fully recused himself from all contracts and obligations related to detention.”

The letter to Warren, sent Thursday, did not share specifics about ICE’s contracting process. Venturella added that he has “complied with all ethics requirements” and fully disclosed his employment with Geo Group before he was hired to work with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

“In the circumstance where contracts may be awarded, this process will be done so in alignment with all relevant federal laws and regulations, while also considering vendors who are best suited for delivery of performance requirements,” he wrote regarding his assurance that he will recuse himself from matters that would benefit Geo Group.

Venturella replaced Todd Lyons, who served as ICE’s acting director until May. Venturella served as his top adviser since 2025, but he previously worked at Geo Group, one of the country’s largest private prison operators, from 2012 to 2023.

Geo Group agreed to house thousands of detained migrants in facilities in New Jersey, Michigan and Georgia that were not previously in use, along with reopening an ICE facility in California, The Wall Street Journal reported. These reopened prisons are under contracts the Trump administration signed last year.

Geo Group has had among the best-performing stocks in 2026, with shares up 82 percent, the Journal reported in June.

Warren replied to Venturella on Sunday, accusing him of leaving “key loopholes” in his recusals.

“Transparency into the agency’s decisions –– and its ties to Geo Group –– is more important than ever, yet your refusal to fully answer all questions about this matter –– in addition to the gaps in your recusal commitments –– only add to the cloud of corruption surrounding ICE and this administration’s immigration agenda,” she wrote in her letter.

Warren requested more information and asked whether Venturella holds stocks in other private prison companies, including CoreCivic.

Among CoreCivic’s prisons used by ICE is the California City Immigration Processing Center, the largest detention center in the Golden State. A court-appointed monitor last week found that the detention center violated a court order to provide adequate medical care to detained migrants and neglected their medical needs.

A CoreCivic spokesperson told The Hill last week that while the company does not “generally comment on matters involving active litigation,” it is reviewing the report into the facility.

President Trump in June nominated Lance Schroyer to be ICE’s permanent director. No confirmation hearing has been scheduled.

The Senate has not confirmed a director to lead ICE since 2017.

In addition to disenfranchising eligible voters, the Executive Order creates confusion and doubt for all eligible voters seeking to mail in their ballots.
“This Executive Order is a naked attempt to keep too many Americans from voting.
Executive Order 14399 is the latest step in the administration’s effort to undermine voter confidence in the elections and create widespread confusion and, ultimately, disenfranchise voters.
Millions of Americans—voters of color, naturalized citizens, elderly voters, voters with limited English proficiency, and voters with disabilities—rely on voting by mail.
text:
SAN FRANCISCO – Asian Law Caucus, Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund, Asian Americans Advancing Justice - Atlanta, Missouri Voter Protection Coalition, South Asian American Justice Collaborative, and Common Cause today filed an amicus brief in the United States Supreme Court on the behalf of 24 organizations urging the Court to reject the Trump administration’s request to reinstate Executive Order 14399 while litigation continues. The filing comes after a federal court blocked key provisions of the Executive Order and the Trump administration and intervenor states asked the Supreme Court to allow its implementation while the case proceeds. With the November midterm elections only months away, civil rights and community organizations are alarmed by the Executive Order, which would undermine access to the ballot, potentially disenfranchising tens of millions of American voters, and bring federal interference into state elections administration. Many of these organizations have spent decades providing direct services and conducting voter outreach and education and urge the Supreme Court to deny the stay of the lower court’s decision invalidating the main sections of the Executive Order. In addition to disenfranchising eligible voters, the Executive Order creates confusion and doubt for all eligible voters seeking to mail in their ballots.

“This Executive Order is a naked attempt to keep too many Americans from voting. Almost half of Asian American voters cast their ballots by mail and many Americans could have their essential right to vote thrown out by a faulty federal system,” said Aarti Kohli, executive director at Asian Law Caucus. “While the Trump administration manufactures yet another crisis, the Asian Law Caucus and our coalition partners are doing the real work of protecting our democracy by training and deploying poll monitors, running an election day hotline, and staying in direct communication with local election officials. Every eligible voter gets to have a say, and we will continue to defend the right to vote.”

“For many voters—especially Asian Americans, naturalized citizens, disabled folks, and voters with limited English proficiency—mail ballot voting is the most practical, and often only way, to cast their vote and participate in our democracy,” said Ronak Patel, staff attorney with the Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund (AALDEF). The federal government's attempt to control states' vote-by-mail programs fails its supposed objectives of protecting against violations of federal law and maintaining public confidence in elections. Instead, it has caused confusion among voters and jeopardized the franchise of millions of American citizens.”

"Trump’s Executive Order directs the Department of Homeland Security to create ‘Citizenship Lists’. This is dangerous because federal databases like SAVE are often incomplete, and SAVE data has resulted in thousands of failures to correctly identify citizens," said Meredyth Yoon, litigation director at Asian Americans Advancing Justice - Atlanta. "The EO threatens to block many eligible voters who rely on voting by mail from casting their ballots, including voters with limited mobility or English proficiency. We are asking the Supreme Court to uphold the status quo by allowing the stay to remain in effect. The real danger of blocking citizens from voting is far worse than the prospect of noncitizens voting, which evidence consistently shows is a non-issue."

Inaccurate, federally-compiled “state citizenship lists” risk disenfranchising eligible voters

Despite clear evidence that noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare, the Trump administration continues to dedicate immense resources to scrutinizing state elections officials. Executive Order instructs the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Social Security Administration (SSA) to compile “‘state citizenship lists” that would use the unreliable federal SAVE database, which the federal government concedes is both incomplete and inaccurate. The federal system has a history of errors and leaves many groups vulnerable to losing their ability to vote due to federal bureaucratic errors—including naturalized citizens, members of communities that have historically experienced discrimination in voting, older individuals, voters with disabilities, voters who are low-income, without access to documentation of their citizenship status or who regularly move and change addresses.

Mail-in ballot changes create confusion and obstacles for voters

The Executive Order also orders the United States Postal Service (USPS) to withhold ballots to voters who do not appear on the lists compiled by DHS and SSA. Tasking three agencies with the power to decide who can vote and who receives a ballot is an extreme departure, as state elections officials maintain constitutional authority to run elections. Executive Order 14399 is the latest step in the administration’s effort to undermine voter confidence in the elections and create widespread confusion and, ultimately, disenfranchise voters. Millions of Americans—voters of color, naturalized citizens, elderly voters, voters with limited English proficiency, and voters with disabilities—rely on voting by mail. For organizations that conduct voter outreach and education, the confusion caused by the Executive Order has added an additional burden as they address voter concerns and ensure that their communities can cast their ballots.

text:
WASHINGTON — More than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children Monday lost their legal representation because the Trump administration has not entered into a new agreement to take over their legal services after it let a longstanding contract with a nonprofit expire.

Without legal representation, fewer than 10% of immigrant children win the right to remain in the United States while their case goes through immigration court. Immigration attorneys and advocates worry the loss in legal aid will put children on a fast track to deportations.

“Right now we're all in the dark, and the secrecy is a big part of the problem,” said Shaina Aber, the executive director of the Acacia Center for Justice, which previously held the contract that expired July 31.

The Department of Health and Human Services, which issues the contract, did not respond to several emails from States Newsroom asking which new organization will take over legal services in immigration courts for unaccompanied kids.

HHS has also not submitted any request for new contractors to provide legal services to unaccompanied minors, according to a States Newsroom review of the federal government’s website for contracts.

Additionally, Scott Ehlers, the director of the Texas Indigent Defense Commission, an organization that the Trump administration was initially eyeing to take over legal services for unaccompanied minors, told States Newsroom it had not been awarded a contract from HHS and had not been contacted by the department regarding one.

Aber said that HHS has not informed Acacia who the new contractor will be, implemented a transition of children’s cases to new attorneys, or paid the organization for completed legal work since December.

HHS has not reimbursed $65 million to Acacia, which distributes the federal funding to roughly 100 organizations across the country who provide legal representation to unaccompanied children in immigration cases.

Struggle over sensitive information

The Trump administration let the contract with Acacia expire after attorneys refused to hand over sensitive case information about their clients, such as whether a child has a pending visa.

Aber said since January, immigration attorneys have seen government attorneys try to use visa information in order to place children in deportation proceedings.

“The government has come up with this novel idea that they're using in the immigration court proceedings that if a visa is pending for a child, that means it's purely speculative that the child would ever have status, and therefore they are ordering deportations for kids who actually have pending T visas, that's a trafficking visa, kids who have pending special immigrant juvenile status, kids with U visas,” she said. “All of those kids are being ordered removed by the courts, even as their visas are awaiting them.”

U nonimmigrant status, or U visas, are set aside for immigrants 21 and younger who were the victim of a crime, or helped provide information to prosecutors about criminal activity.

Separately, a special immigrant juvenile status is extended to immigrant children who have been “abandoned, abused, or neglected” by a parent, and that visa provides a pathway for a green card.

A nonprofit in Pennsylvania, the Jewish Family and Community Services of Pittsburgh, recently filed a lawsuit on behalf of several immigrant children against the Trump administration’s practice of targeting children with pending visas for deportation.

Aber said she is worried that the next organization to obtain the contract will hand over that sensitive information to the Trump administration.

“We are very concerned about any agreement that the government has entered into with a new contractor about sharing confidential details or privileged information contrary to children's interests,” she said.

Confusion about legal services

Aber said HHS is still working on accepting a transition proposal, meaning that Acacia and providers in its network cannot even begin having conversations with children to inform them that someone else will be representing them in immigration court.

“To have those really sensitive conversations with the child, where you're saying, ‘Hey, I'm not going to be able to represent you anymore, or like these are your options in terms of representation’ …. we can't start having those conversations with kids without that information,” she said.

She added that officials at the Office of Refugee and Resettlement, the agency within HHS that houses some unaccompanied immigrant children, are still reaching out to Acacia and its legal services providers even after the contract expired, asking for legal services for newly arrived children. Almost 1,800 children are in ORR’s care, according to agency data from June.

“They keep on reaching out to our legal service services network, asking if someone could please go over on their own dime to talk to new arriving children,” Aber said.

Some of the organizations that partner with Acacia have been able to dip into reserves to continue providing services to kids, but others have had to stop providing the services altogether, Aber said.
