text:
This spring, each man’s plans unraveled in a sudden, similar way. Federal officers detained them during routine check-ins with immigration authorities, traffic stops and raids as part of the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. On June 24, they were shackled and placed aboard a plane back to Venezuela.

Across the South American nation, relatives prepared to welcome them home. Some bought balloons. Some cooked favorite meals. Others got in their cars and headed to greet the deportees when they landed at Simón Bolívar International Airport.

But there were no reunions that day. Instead, Venezuelan officials loaded the group of 146 deportees — including 19 women and seven children — onto buses and drove them to Hotel Santuario La Llanada, a secluded government facility perched on a hillside in the coastal state of La Guaira. Hours later, two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela in what now ranks as one of nation’s deadliest natural disasters on record. More than 5,500 people were killed, nearly 17,000 were injured and the United Nations estimates that upward of 50,000 are still missing.

The four-story building where the immigrants were being kept toppled into a pile of broken concrete, twisted metal and dust.

Neither the Venezuelan government nor the Trump administration has publicly released a complete passenger manifest. Nor have officials explained why deportees were taken into custody by the Bolivarian National Intelligence Service (SEBIN), the state security agency that has been accused of human rights violations, and what happened to them.

The Washington Post sought to find out who the immigrants were and how they ended up on Flight 164, interviewing relatives of 16 passengers ― most of whom are now dead or missing ― three survivors, human rights experts and Venezuelan officials, and reviewing videos, photographs, text messages and other documents.

Most of those whose cases were reconstructed had pending asylum claims when they were detained, their relatives said. About half had been shielded from deportation through temporary protected status until the Trump administration canceled that benefit for Venezuelans last year.

Several of the passengers told their families they were hoping to continue pursuing their immigration cases but ultimately agreed to be deported after weeks or months in ICE detention.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to requests for information about who was on the flight and denied accusations that detainees are pressured to voluntarily deport.

“This flight safely reached Venezuela and all illegal aliens on board were returned home,” the agency said in a written statement. “When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them.”

Venezuela’s Ministry of Communication and Information did not respond to requests for information about the deportees, why they were taken into custody and what happened to them. They also did not comment on accusations that officials have provided confusing and in some cases incorrect information to relatives about whether their loved ones survived.

The families said they were left to search on their own for answers. The ruins of Hotel Santuario La Llanada remain under the control of Venezuela’s intelligence police and have been closed off to family members, rescue groups and the media. Relatives of the deportees have spent weeks seeking information through leaked passenger lists, cellphone videos, text messages, phone calls, and visits to hospitals and morgues. Several relatives said SEBIN officers warned them not to speak publicly.

“They failed us,” said Daniely Hurtado, the wife of Osal Mujica, the former Venezuelan police officer. She blamed the U.S. government for what she described as psychological torture in detention and the Venezuelan government for negligence after the earthquakes. “It was an irreparable failure.”

Arrests and detention

Since arriving in the United States in 2023, Osal Mujica had repaired roofs, cleaned water tanks and made deliveries around Denver, sending money home to pay for household expenses and his son’s schooling. He applied for asylum and obtained a work permit. But he missed an immigration court date when the summons paperwork went to an old address.

When Denver became saturated with immigrant workers, many of whom had also crossed the U.S. border during the Biden administration, Osal Mujica started looking for opportunities in Wyoming. He had a Colorado-issued driver’s license, his wife said, and found work making deliveries. He did not know Wyoming does not recognize state licenses issued to drivers without a legal status, she said.

“‘I’ll give myself one year,’” Hurtado recalled her husband saying. “He never wanted to be there, but he went to help his family.”

A sheriff’s deputy stopped Osal Mujica, 32, while he was driving in April. In Wyoming and across the country, local agencies were increasingly cooperating with ICE to carry out immigration enforcement. He was taken into custody and immediately signed a voluntary departure order, his wife said.

In early May, he withdrew his asylum claim and told a court he would not appeal a removal order. But his detention dragged on and he grew increasingly anxious and depressed.

Osal Mujica told his wife that the lights were kept on at all hours and that he struggled to sleep. During one video call, he showed his son a bleeding scar where he had etched the boy’s name into his arm with a blade he had stolen. Hurtado scolded him, terrified. He later went on a hunger strike, begging authorities to let him go. He lost 60 pounds.

Hurtado said officials told her husband they had lost his papers. Later, detention officers said he would have to pay for his own flight home. His family deposited money into his account, but weeks went by with no word of when he would return.

DHS did not comment on Hurtado’s accusations, saying only in a statement that Osal Mujica had entered the country illegally and that the Transportation Security Administration had caught him using a fraudulent Social Security number in November 2023. His family said he had been duped by someone he believed was an attorney shortly after arriving in the United States and thought it was a valid number.

“He told his sister, ‘If they don’t release me, I don’t know what I’m going to do,’” Hurtado recalled through sobs. Mujica went on to lament to his wife: “I was just working. Why are they making me suffer like this?”

Similar stories of arrest and detention were unfolding across the country. While DHS was not staging large-scale federal immigration deployments like the ones it conducted in Minneapolis and Chicago over the past year, officers were still making hundreds of arrests each day. The men and women who would eventually find themselves on Flight 164 were among those detained in a wave of apprehensions that rarely made headlines.

In May, a Mother’s Day traffic stop in Jacksonville, Florida, resulted in the arrest of Daniel Alejandro Nuñez Ramirez, 28, whose family said he had a pending asylum claim. Three days later, Broward County sheriff’s deputies descended on a Home Depot where day laborers gathered looking for work and detained 29-year-old Yonaiker José Ortiz Lara, who had no legal status. In New Jersey, Jhonattan Lamus, 40, received a notice directing him to report to immigration authorities to regularize his immigration status. He had received temporary protected status but, like other Venezuelans, now faced the possibility of removal after it was canceled.

“Instead of going into hiding, as many people did, he decided to show up and follow the law,” said Adela Osuna, Lamus’s cousin. “Part of him wanted to go back to Venezuela, and he jokingly said to us, ‘Well, if they deport me, even better — I save myself the price of the plane ticket.’”

By June, ICE officers had begun to dramatically increase arrests as part of a new enforcement surge.

In Chicago, immigration officers arrested Villegas Castillo, 37, the former fisherman, after entering a house where he was doing construction work, his sister said. On June 13, Florida Highway Patrol stopped landscaper Luis Alberto Marchán Hernández, 27, while he was driving a work truck near Orlando. A week later, immigration officers arrested Yamilk Alberto Caldera, 32, and his wife as they made food deliveries in Tucson.

Pereira Amesty, 34, and his wife were summoned to check in with ICE in Tennessee in June. They had obtained and then lost temporary protected status shielding them from deportation but were still pursuing an asylum claim. Officers gave the couple a choice, their niece said: One of them could be detained while fighting their immigration case, or they could both sign paperwork agreeing to leave the country with their son.

The family agreed to voluntarily deport, and was told they’d have until August to buy plane tickets and pack their belongings. But when they went to a check-in a week later, officers told the family they’d be leaving that day, their niece said, and immediately took them into custody.

Other families were separated. Ortiz Lara, who was arrested at the Broward County Home Depot, texted his partner from Camp East Montana, a notorious tent city at Fort Bliss, Texas, where many of the migrants who would eventually board Flight 164 were being held.

“Esto es duro,” he texted his partner, who shared the texts on the condition of anonymity because she fears being targeted by authorities in the U.S. and Venezuela. “This is really hard.”

The couple made a plan. Ortiz Lara’s partner and their toddler would surrender to federal immigration officers and request deportation so they could rebuild their lives together in Caracas.

The night before his flight home, Ortiz Lara sent one final message.

“Nos vemos en Venezuela.”

We’ll see each other in Venezuela.

Flying home

Jeycibeth Montiel Nava felt torn as she boarded the plane in El Paso.

The 31-year-old mother of three had fled Venezuela after receiving threats tied to her family’s involvement in local politics. She applied for asylum in 2023 and believed a judge would recognize the merits of her case and offer her a path toward citizenship. But weeks inside Georgia’s Stewart Detention Center had worn her down. She said guards yelled obscenities at the detainees, denied them bathroom breaks and served them bowls of food like beans that had worms.

She withdrew her asylum claim and signed papers agreeing to return voluntarily. Going back meant seeing her children again. It also meant giving up on the future she had imagined in the United States.

Women and children were assigned seats together in one part of the plane, and men placed in another. The adults were shackled at the wrists and ankles.

“We were happy to go after all of the abuse,” she recalled. “But we thought we’d be free.”

When the flight landed in Venezuela, passengers were greeted by government officials and television cameras.

Venezuela’s Return to the Homeland Mission, the government initiative charged with processing deportees, posted photographs and video celebrating the migrants’ arrival. Officials embraced passengers and handed toys to children. They referred to the plane as Flight 164, the government’s tally of deportation flights from the United States and other countries.

Since the program’s creation in 2018, the government has portrayed it as a humanitarian mission, welcoming Venezuelans home after hardships abroad. At the same time, government officials have frequently accused migrants of being manipulated by foreign powers and cast suspicion on those who leave the country.

“When the cameras are rolling, they hug you,” said one deportee, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of security concerns. “But once that’s done, they treat you like you’re a traitor for leaving the country.”

SEBIN agents loaded most of the Flight 164 passengers onto buses headed for Hotel Santuario La Llanada.

The terracotta-roofed compound overlooking the Caribbean had never operated as a hotel. Built around 1960 as a Catholic primary and high school, it later housed a “city of youth” where residents attended school, learned trades and performed in a renowned traveling circus. The Venezuelan government eventually converted the property into a residential drug rehabilitation center and, during the coronavirus pandemic, a quarantine facility.

After Iceland deported a group of Venezuelans in 2024, SEBIN used the facility to process returnees before releasing them to their families. Flight 164’s passengers would follow the same route.

“They told us we were being detained because we are under investigation for 24 hours before they deliver us to our families,” Montiel Nava recalled. “I don’t know why they needed to take us there.”

Officials issued new national identity cards and instructed the deportees to find bags labeled with their names that contained their belongings. But SEBIN agents collected people’s phones and demanded the passwords, several survivors said.

One man said an agent told him officials were looking for evidence that deportees opposed the government. If they found it, the agent warned, they could be detained longer.

Deportees were allowed to make a single phone call home — with a phone provided by a SEBIN officer. Before dialing, they had to give the name, national identification number, address and cellphone number of the relative they wanted to contact, survivors said.

Officials assigned the deportees to rooms lined with bunk beds and told them they could not leave except to use the bathroom under escort, deportees said. They distributed towels and toiletries, turned on the water so everyone could shower, then brought meals to the rooms.

Montiel Nava said she was one of the last of the women to be processed for her national identification documents. She went to her room on the second floor, lay down and started drifting to sleep with her Bible tucked underneath her pillow.

Around 6 p.m., screams startled her awake. Everything shook. The walls around her began to collapse. Debris smashed the metal frame of the bunk bed she was resting in and came within inches of crushing her.

“I could hear people screaming and crying,” Montiel Nava said. “To get out, I had to climb over the piece of cement that had crushed to death the woman who was next to my bed.”

Nine women crawled out an opening in the pancaked roof to safety, she said.

Montiel Nava said that she asked some of the intelligence officers to help them rescue those still inside but that they did not respond to her pleas. Dazed and shoeless, she started walking as night fell.

For four hours, she trekked past what she described as a nightmare reel of pulverized cement, headless children and crushed bodies. She arrived at a Venezuelan National Guard command post where people were beginning to assemble an open-air morgue.

A soldier brought her an arepa to eat.

Searching the rubble

Far from Caracas, in the small town of El Mecocal, one deportee’s mother was carefully writing “Welcome Home” on a banner when news about the earthquakes began to spread.

As the hours passed, she began to worry.

She knew her son, Arturo, was being held by the government after landing near the epicenter of the disaster. The Post agreed to identify Arturo by only his first name and withhold his mother’s identity because the family fears retribution in Venezuela. He fled the country in 2023 to help support his mother and her work as a seamstress.

Arturo’s town quickly rallied to find him. On June 26, a convoy of motorcycles and cars loaded with food, water and medical supplies left from the western state of Zulia and began the 16-hour drive toward La Guaira.

They arrived at dawn. But SEBIN officers had sealed off the site of the collapsed building. Families were barred from entering, and many were threatened with detention, said the leader of Arturo’s convoy, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation.

Relatives of residents from other destroyed buildings could sometimes find their loved ones in morgues and intensive care units by searching for people found at a certain address. But many of Flight 164’s family members did not know exactly where they had been taken, and said the deportees at most were labeled “repatriados” — repatriated.

Arturo’s search party eventually received word that his body had been found in a Caracas morgue. When they arrived, he wasn’t there. Then came another call from an improvised morgue at the Port of La Guaira. His mother recognized him by the tattoo stretched across his ribs: “Family. Where life begins and where love never ends.”

Other families of the deportees said they received confusing and at times contradictory information.

Intelligence agents twice visited the home of Adela Osuna’s uncle in the state of Táchira, she said. During one visit, they offered condolences, telling the family that her cousin, Jhonattan Lamus, had died. The next time, they told the family to stop talking publicly about his case.

A week later, however, a SEBIN official scrolled through what Osuna believed was a passenger list on his cellphone before telling her Lamus was not among those recovered from the rubble. Perhaps, he suggested, her cousin had wandered away after the earthquake. Perhaps he had amnesia. Perhaps he was in shock. She should keep checking hospitals.

“They’re the ones who took him there” to Hotel Santuario La Llanada, Osuna said later. “They’re the ones who should be looking for him.”

Orly Guzmán found her son Andrés Contreras alive at Pérez Carreño Hospital in Caracas three days after the earthquake. While sitting beside his hospital bed, she said, she received a phone call from SEBIN offering condolences because her son had supposedly been found dead.

“They simply have no idea who is alive and who isn’t,” she said.

Another family, speaking on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, said SEBIN officials offered to provide proof that their loved one was alive in exchange for $100. The next day, they said, they began receiving messages asking for more money to feed and care for him.

Four days after the earthquake, they found his body in a morgue.

The secrecy extended beyond the deportees. Venezuelan authorities have never publicly acknowledged that SEBIN officers also died in the collapse. But one intelligence officer, speaking on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss the disaster, told The Post that at least 20 of his colleagues were buried beneath the rubble.

Montiel Nava said the silence surrounding the fate of her fellow Flight 164 passengers has compounded the pain.

“They hid our story,” she said. “They hid us. No one mentioned Flight 164. Families had to work on their own to find out what happened to their loved ones. … Not President Trump and not the Venezuelan government mentioned or talked about us.”

Some families have stayed behind in Caracas and La Guaira, hoping each new lead might finally tell them what happened. Jhonattan Lamus’s family doesn’t own a car, but relatives have been taking turns making the 12-hour trek by bus to the capital every week. He still has not been found.

“We just want closure at this point,” Osuna said. “We need to know where he is.”

An unknown toll

One month after the earthquakes, the Venezuelan government has not disclosed how many of the deportees died and how many are still buried beneath the hotel.

Pereira Amesty was pulled from the rubble alive but gravely injured. He was taken to a hospital, where he died. His wife and their young son clawed their way out of the collapsed building. SEBIN officers took them back into custody and later drove them to their family’s home.

It took Osal Mujica’s wife five days to find her husband’s remains.

Authorities sent her from hospitals to the morgue, blocked her from entering Hotel Santuario La Llanada and, at one point, presented her with a body that was not his. Eventually her sister-in-law in the United States obtained a photograph of a decomposing body, and Hurtado recognized by Osal Mujica’s Dragon Ball Z tattoo and the bracelet U.S. deportation officers had placed on his wrist.

Hurtado went to retrieve the body. In a pants pocket, she found her husband’s deportation order, folded and stained with dust from debris. She wrapped it in plastic. That was the document he had spent months anxiously waiting to receive. She wanted to keep something he had longed for.

María José Villegas Castillo traveled to La Guaira by boat from her family’s hometown in hopes of bringing her brother home. She found his remains three days after the earthquakes. His face had swollen beyond recognition, but she recognized his body by the Chinese characters tattooed along his ribs.

His family cremated his remains and gathered with friends to bid the fisherman farewell.

They built an altar draped with Venezuelan and American flags. As tambores — traditional Afro-Venezuelan drums played at celebrations and funerals — echoed across the gathering, relatives poured a splash of anís liquor over the urn before carrying it aboard a waiting fishing boat.

They scattered Villegas Castillo’s ashes into the Caribbean. The fisherman who had crossed continents trying to provide for his children returned to the sea without ever making it home.

His youngest daughter still has not accepted that he is gone.

“She says she wants to die,” Villegas Castillo’s sister said quietly, “because she wants to stay in the sea with her daddy.”

text:
LOS ANGELES — Immigrants traveling within the United States are facing an increased risk of detention at airports, including individuals previously considered relatively safe to fly domestically, prompting the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, to issue a rare travel advisory this week following reports of arrests by immigration agents at airports nationwide.

Yunuen Trujillo, immigration attorney and director of Workers’ Rights Legal Services at the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, stated:

“Over the past several weeks, CHIRLA has received reports from community members indicating an increase in immigration-related detentions at U.S. airports during domestic travel. We have confirmed multiple reports of these detentions occurring at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO) in California. Similar incidents have also been reported in Nevada, Colorado, Massachusetts, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Michigan, New Jersey, Texas, and Virginia.”

Trujillo further added that these incidents, unlike previously reported immigration enforcement during domestic air travel, show a pattern of affecting individuals who may not have been considered at high risk for domestic flying in the past.

The reported detentions have included individuals who overstayed a visa or violated their visa terms — regardless of whether they have a criminal history, prior removal orders or pending immigration proceedings.

Detentions, the press release notes, have been occurring during layovers on domestic flights. People have also been detained even if they have pending applications for immigration relief, are in a period of authorized stay or have valid employment authorization.

Because of these reports, CHIRLA urges people to be careful when determining whether it is appropriate to travel domestically.

Trujillo stated that community members need to thoroughly evaluate whether it is necessary to travel at this time, and he encourages people to consult with a qualified immigration attorney before traveling to assess their specific cases and determine the potential risk.

Trujillo and his team especially recommended that individuals with pending green card applications or asylum applications check with an attorney to determine whether it is safe for them to travel domestically.

He suggested that these people postpone their nonessential domestic travel plans until they have consulted with an attorney and created a travel plan for their specific circumstances.

According to an article by NBC Los Angeles, there is no clear indication of when this travel advisory will end or when immigrants can resume domestic travel. Additionally, this travel advisory is different from past advisories because of the multitude of reasons for the arrests.

People who seem to be safe to travel are still being detained, the press release noted, reflecting uncertainty about the basis on which these arrests are being made.

In addition to precautions for domestic travel, the release explains that, to obtain referrals or seek trusted legal immigration consultation, the public is urged to contact the national Immigrant Assistance Hotline at (888) 624-4752.

CHIRLA was founded in 1986 to advance the human and civil rights of immigrants and refugees. CHIRLA became a place for organizations and people who support human rights to work together on policies that advance justice and full inclusion for all immigrants.

CHIRLA has since become one of the largest and most effective advocates for immigrant rights, organizing, educating and defending immigrants and refugees in the streets, in the courts and in the halls of power. Its main goal is to ensure the protection of people from all backgrounds and end exclusion within public systems.

text:
Key Highlights

A federal appeals court on July 24, 2026, rejected the Trump administration‘s request to reinstate a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas, marking another legal setback in the president’s effort to reshape the high-skilled foreign worker program.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit declined to pause a June 8 ruling by U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin of the District of Massachusetts, who blocked the fee in a lawsuit brought by 20 Democratic state attorneys general.

A three-judge panel denied the administration’s request, finding that the government had not shown it was likely to succeed in its appeal.

The decision means U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the State Department cannot collect the $100,000 charge on qualifying H-1B petitions while the broader legal fight continues.

What the court found

The First Circuit concluded that the administration failed to demonstrate a strong likelihood of winning its appeal.

The Trump administration argued in a June 12 motion that the fee was a lawful exercise of presidential authority over immigration and foreign commerce. The appeals court rejected that argument, leaving intact Sorokin’s finding that the charge operated as an unauthorized tax.

The ruling followed a brief procedural pause after Sorokin’s decision. The district court temporarily allowed the government to continue collecting the fee while the administration sought emergency relief from the First Circuit. The July 24 order ended that pause and restored the block.

The President’s original justification

Donald Trump signed Proclamation 10973, titled “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers,” on September 19, 2025.

In the proclamation, Trump argued that the H-1B program was intended for temporary, high-skilled workers but had been exploited by companies to replace American employees with lower-paid foreign labor. He said widespread misuse of the program threatened economic and national security and justified imposing higher costs on employers.

A White House fact sheet released alongside the proclamation claimed that U.S. technology companies were “laying off their American technology workers and seemingly replacing them with H-1B workers.”

The fact sheet cited an increase in the share of H-1B workers employed in the information technology sector, rising from about 32 percent in 2003 to more than 65 percent in recent years.

Why the case matters

The legal dispute centers on whether a president can impose a fee of this size on a federal visa program without explicit approval from Congress.

Judge Sorokin ruled that the $100,000 charge functioned as a tax rather than a regulatory fee. Under the Constitution, Congress holds the power to levy taxes and establish immigration policy.

Twenty states, led by California, challenged the fee, arguing that the administration exceeded presidential authority by imposing the charge without congressional approval.

Financial stakes for employers

Before the proclamation, employers generally paid between $2,000 and $5,000 to obtain H-1B visas.

Congress limits the program to 65,000 regular visas annually, with an additional 20,000 available for workers holding advanced degrees.

The $100,000 fee took effect on September 21, 2025 and applied only to new H-1B petitions involving workers subject to consular processing — meaning applicants seeking visas from outside the United States.

The fee did not apply to foreign nationals already in the U.S., including many international students transitioning from student visas to H-1B status.

What comes next

The First Circuit’s July 24 decision was procedural and did not resolve the underlying appeal.

The Trump administration can continue fighting the case before the appeals court, which will eventually decide the broader legal questions surrounding the fee. If the administration loses, it could ask the Supreme Court to review the case, though the justices are not required to take it.

title: Why linguistic profiling in an era of migration and tension makes no sense - Daily Maverick
description:

Setswana is spoken not only in South Africa, but also by large populations in Botswana and parts of Namibia and Zimbabwe.
As a result, many African language communities today are distributed across several sovereign states.
Those who speak with unfamiliar accents, belong to minority language communities or simply fail arbitrary linguistic “tests” may also become targets.
His perspective on migration, identity and human rights is informed by his lived experience across national and cultural environments.
text:
Anyone who has lived in South Africa has probably witnessed it. A person walks into a shop in Cape Town and is immediately asked, “Where are you really from?” because of their accent.

A job applicant in Durban finds themselves treated with suspicion after speaking isiZulu with a different regional inflection. A commuter on a taxi in Johannesburg is questioned – or even harassed – for speaking Shona, Chichewa or French.

Across the country, accent and language have increasingly become informal tests of belonging, often shaping how people are perceived, trusted or excluded long before their citizenship or legal status is ever established.

These everyday encounters reveal a deeper social reality: in South Africa, language is often treated not simply as a means of communication, but as a marker of identity, nationality and legitimacy.

Yet language and accent are imperfect and unreliable indicators of who people are. They reflect histories of migration, education, family background, multilingualism and cultural interaction far more than they reveal legal citizenship or national identity.

Against this backdrop, the recent statement by the Pan South African Language Board that “an accent is not an identity” raises an important human rights and governance issue that extends beyond South Africa’s current migration debates.

It addresses a broader global challenge: the tendency to use language, pronunciation, ethnicity, appearance or cultural expression as informal indicators of nationality, belonging or legal status.

While concerns surrounding undocumented migration are legitimate policy matters requiring effective governance, effective border management and lawful administrative processes, these challenges cannot be addressed through assumptions based on linguistic identity. The use of language or accent as a measure of nationality is historically inaccurate, legally problematic and socially divisive.

In a country built on multilingualism, constitutional equality and freedom of movement, reducing identity to the way someone speaks risks undermining the very values that South Africa’s democratic order seeks to protect.

Language has never followed political borders

One of the greatest misconceptions in contemporary debates about migration and identity is the assumption that language neatly corresponds with nationality.

History tells a very different story.

Languages have never respected political borders because, for most of human history, the borders themselves did not exist. Instead, languages spread through migration, trade, conquest, intermarriage, pastoral movements and cultural exchange, creating linguistic landscapes that long predate the establishment of modern nation-states.

The history of the Nguni languages provides a compelling example. Between about the eleventh and seventeenth centuries, Bantu-speaking communities gradually migrated southwards from the Great Lakes region of East and Central Africa through present-day Mozambique into what is now South Africa.

These movements were neither singular nor uniform; they occurred over several centuries through successive waves of migration, settlement and interaction with existing communities. As these populations expanded, their languages evolved into the Nguni language family, including isiZulu, isiXhosa, isiNdebele and siSwati. These languages share a common linguistic ancestry, explaining their high degree of mutual intelligibility while also reflecting the diverse historical experiences of the communities that speak them.

The nineteenth-century Mfecane (or Difaqane) further transformed the linguistic map of Southern Africa. Political upheavals, warfare and the establishment of new kingdoms resulted in significant population movements across the region.

Communities associated with the expanding Zulu kingdom migrated into present-day Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Eswatini, Malawi and Zambia, giving rise to new settlements and linguistic communities. The Northern Ndebele, for example, established themselves in present-day Zimbabwe under Mzilikazi, while other Nguni-speaking groups settled across neighbouring countries.

These historical processes ensured that related Nguni languages became established across much of southern Africa, centuries before the colonial partition of Africa.

The same pattern is evident among other southern African language groups.

Setswana is spoken not only in South Africa, but also by large populations in Botswana and parts of Namibia and Zimbabwe. Sesotho extends across South Africa and Lesotho, where it is one of the official languages, while Sepedi, Tshivenda and Xitsonga are also spoken across borders with Zimbabwe and Mozambique.

Similarly, Chichewa, Shona and Portuguese are heard in many South African towns and cities because migration across the region has long been part of southern Africa’s social and economic history. These are not foreign intrusions into a fixed linguistic landscape; they are the continuation of centuries-old patterns of regional mobility and cultural exchange.

Colonialism further complicated these linguistic geographies. The borders drawn by European colonial powers during the late nineteenth century – formalised at the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 – paid little attention to existing cultural, linguistic or ethnic landscapes.

Communities that had lived together for generations found themselves divided between different colonies, while others were incorporated into entirely new political entities. As a result, many African language communities today are distributed across several sovereign states. National boundaries may separate countries, but they rarely separate languages or cultures.

Even within South Africa, language has never been geographically fixed. Urbanisation, labour migration, apartheid-era forced removals and post-1994 internal migration have created highly multilingual communities where people routinely speak several languages and adopt accents influenced by education, family background and the places in which they have lived. A person born in Limpopo may grow up in Durban, study in Cape Town and work in Johannesburg, developing a linguistic identity that reflects multiple regions rather than a single locality.

For these reasons, expecting a person’s accent, pronunciation or vocabulary to conform to a narrowly defined national identity fundamentally misunderstands how languages evolve.

Language is shaped by centuries of human mobility, social interaction and cultural adaptation – not by passport offices or immigration checkpoints.

Accents reveal stories of migration, education, family history and multilingualism; they do not reveal citizenship or legal status.

Using language or accent as a proxy for nationality is therefore both historically inaccurate and socially harmful. It ignores the deeply interconnected histories of African societies and reduces complex identities to superficial markers of speech. In a region where languages have crossed landscapes long before political borders were drawn, linguistic diversity should be recognised as evidence of our shared history rather than treated as grounds for suspicion or exclusion.

The danger of linguistic profiling

The emergence of the “Abahambe” movement, spearheaded by groups such as March and March, has intensified the linguistic debate. While many supporters frame the campaign as a response to legitimate concerns about undocumented migration, pressure on public services and weaknesses in border management, there is a real danger when public frustration becomes translated into informal systems of identifying who “belongs”, based on how they speak.

When ordinary citizens assume the role of determining nationality through language, the line between civic activism and discrimination becomes increasingly blurred.

Linguistic profiling is particularly dangerous because it relies on assumptions rather than evidence. It reduces complex identities to a single observable characteristic, ignoring the realities of multilingualism, internal migration and regional mobility.

A South African born and raised in Cape Town may speak isiXhosa differently from someone in Mthatha. A Setswana speaker from Mahikeng may sound remarkably similar to someone from Gaborone. An isiZulu speaker from northern KwaZulu-Natal may share linguistic features with communities in Eswatini or southern Mozambique.

None of these differences reveals citizenship; they simply reflect the rich diversity of language communities that have evolved across southern Africa over centuries.

History also reminds us that once societies begin using language or ethnicity as informal tests of belonging, exclusion rarely remains confined to foreign nationals.

Those who speak with unfamiliar accents, belong to minority language communities or simply fail arbitrary linguistic “tests” may also become targets. South Africans themselves can be misidentified, questioned or excluded because they do not conform to someone else’s expectations of what a “real” South African should sound like. In this way, linguistic profiling ultimately threatens everyone living in a multilingual society.

Beyond its immediate human rights implications, this trend poses broader risks for South Africa’s regional and continental aspirations.

South Africa is deeply integrated into the Southern African Development Community, where the movement of people, labour, skills and investment has long underpinned regional development.

Families, businesses and communities routinely span the borders of South Africa, Botswana, Namibia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Lesotho and Eswatini. Languages such as Setswana, Sesotho, siSwati, isiNdebele, Tshivenda and Xitsonga are spoken across these national boundaries, reflecting shared histories rather than separate identities.

If language increasingly becomes a basis for suspicion, South Africa risks undermining not only social cohesion at home, but also the spirit of regional integration that has been central to post-apartheid foreign policy.

Trust between neighbouring countries can be eroded when their citizens are routinely viewed with suspicion because they speak a familiar language differently. Such perceptions may also weaken cooperation on trade, labour mobility, education, tourism and cross-border development – all priorities embedded in regional integration frameworks and the African Union’s vision of a more connected continent. DM

Vukani Chris Mhlanga is a technology executive and entrepreneur whose work spans technology, digital systems and cross-border business development in southern Africa and Europe. His perspective on migration, identity and human rights is informed by his lived experience across national and cultural environments.

Dr Simangele Dlamini is a social sciences researcher and academic, and writes in his personal capacity.

text:
The family of a Haitian immigrant who froze to death in early March at a bus shelter in Pittsburgh after she was dropped off in the city by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is poised to file a lawsuit this month against the United States and “multiple other governmental and non-governmental entities”, the Guardian has learned.

Daphy Michel, 31, had been in county jail for six months after a reported mental health crisis and street incident, and then was arrested by ICE before being released with a ankle monitor.

She was left to make her way home to Charleroi, a small community on the outskirts of Pittsburgh about 20 miles (32km) away, but was found dead three days later. In June, Pennsylvania officials said she died from hypothermia and ruled her death a homicide.

The Allegheny county medical examiner’s office said Michel was a vulnerable adult “suffering from untreated severe mental health issues and a significant language barrier” at the time of her release from federal custody on 27 February.

Attorney Joseph Murphy, who represents members of Michel’s family living locally, said this week that the lawsuit will be filed within the next two to three weeks. He had said at the time of the homicide ruling that relatives in the US were likely to sue.

“Anybody who knew Daphy for more than one minute knew there was something wrong with her. It was a real dumb thing to just release her like that in February in Pittsburgh, where it’s very cold, knowing how screwed up she was. It was a very bad judgment call,” Murphy said.

Relatives and the attorney believe that ICE did not grasp the risks Michel faced being released alone on a city street that was probably unfamiliar to her, especially given the state of her health. The morning she was found unresponsive, she was wearing summer clothes and the temperature was just 20F (-6.6C). There are few details available about the lawsuit so far, including the identities of plaintiffs and defendants.

The medical examiner’s office explained in a statement that its ruling of homicide should not be interpreted as a declaration of criminal guilt but as “actions caused by another individual”. Pittsburgh detectives are now investigating.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, did not respond this week to questions from the Guardian about the impending lawsuit, Michel’s time in its custody or her death. In March, the agency posted a statement on X saying it had “nothing to do with this woman’s death”. It called Michel an illegal alien, although Murphy said she entered the US legally, was awarded humanitarian status and had an asylum application in process.

Surveillance camera images show Michel at the bus shelter on Pittsburgh’s south side, sitting on the bench in daylight at first on 1 March, with a small, pale bag of belongings, still sitting there in darkness that evening, then slumped half upright on the ground and eventually lying on the ground the following morning.

The images were first published by the outlet Pittsburgh’s Public Source, an independent news non-profit that filed legal requests with the local transportation authority and then viewed hours of surveillance video footage showing Michel was at the bus stop for about 24 hours. It shared the images with the Guardian.

After someone made a call, authorities found Michel and attempted lifesaving measures, but she died hours later in a Pittsburgh hospital.

Michel had been arrested by police last September after a member of the public made an emergency call saying she appeared to be having a mental health crisis in the street in Charleroi, which has a substantial Haitian immigrant community. She was screaming, apparently in response to imaginary voices, and brandishing a knife. She was locked up in the Washington county jail to the south-west of Pittsburgh, awaiting court hearings that were repeatedly rescheduled.

A judge eventually dismissed the charges and ordered her freed from jail in late February. She had an immigration hearing a few weeks later, but ICE arrested her and took her in the opposite direction from home, to its office in south Pittsburgh, then released her.

The DHS said previously that it had been sunny and Michel’s phone was fully charged when she was released. But Murphy said Michel’s phone plan had expired while she was in jail.

text:
WASHINGTON — At a tidy Lutheran church near the U.S. Capitol in mid-July, Tereza Lee, a 43-year-old professional musician who has performed at Carnegie Hall and with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, sat at a grand piano near the wooden altar and played a portion of Frédéric Chopin’s iconic “Fantaisie-Impromptu.”

In the pews, more than a dozen well-dressed young Black, Hispanic and Asian men and women gathered for an unusual ceremony. They wore caps and gowns of various colors — mostly black, but also shades of blue and cardinal red — from colleges across the country. One decorated her green cap with flowers, a butterfly and the message: “Dreams without borders. Gracias mami y papi.”

At a place of honor up front sat U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois, an 81-year-old Democratic lawmaker on the verge of retirement, whom many in the room credited for allowing them to attend college, find jobs and start families because of — and this doesn’t happen often — a bill he has for decades tried, but failed, to pass.

The mock-graduation ceremony celebrated those achievements and Durbin’s advocacy for the DREAM Act, legislation that would allow immigrants brought to the U.S. illegally as children to become citizens. Inspired by Lee, Durbin first introduced the measure in 2001, before the September terrorist attacks made talk of immigration reform toxic to many Republicans on Capitol Hill.

In the quarter century since, Durbin has repeatedly reintroduced the measure, recruited new GOP co-sponsors and sought novel strategies to get it signed into law. The DREAM Act has passed the Senate. It has passed the House. But it has not passed the House and Senate in the same year. Still, it has won over most Americans, with a June Gallup poll finding 81% of respondents favored the idea. Durbin’s proposal has prompted more than a dozen states to offer in-state tuition to undocumented students, often through laws explicitly called “DREAM Acts.” It’s also inspired nonprofit scholarship programs, spurred youth-led organizing campaigns, and given rise to the term “dreamer.”

Perhaps most importantly, the DREAM Act became a template for a 2012 program giving temporary reprieve from deportations to more than 800,000 young people, a mechanism still in place today. Durbin pressed President Barack Obama, his former Senate colleague from Illinois, after repeatedly raising concerns about dreamers being deported under Obama’s administration. Obama’s response was the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, which let recipients stay in the country and work legally. President Donald Trump has repeatedly tried to eliminate or shrink DACA, but it still covers roughly 495,000 people, including more than 26,000 in Illinois.

But with less than half a year left in a federal legislative career that began in the House in 1983 and grew to three decades in the Senate, Durbin is coming to terms with the idea that what he describes as his “most important” piece of legislation will not become law.

“I feel sad in a way that I’m retiring without making it the law of the land,” Durbin told the Tribune during a recent interview in his Capitol office. “But it is a tough climate to talk about the DREAM Act and immigration with this current administration.”

Gaby Pacheco, president and CEO of TheDream.US, a leading advocacy group for dreamers, first met Durbin in the mid-2000s. In 2010, she led the “Trail of Dreams” march of undocumented immigrants from Miami to Washington to build support for dreamers and immigration reform. Sixteen years later, she led the mock graduation ceremony in July and said she became emotional preparing remarks to thank Durbin for his efforts.

“I was just crying,” she told her fellow dreamers who gathered at the church, “just thinking about how beautiful it is to have somebody who believes in you, what a beauty it is to know there’s a man who has been fighting for you for 25 years, a man who barely even knew me.”

The senator has long pushed to make the nation’s immigration laws more accommodating. In fact, Durbin keeps the framed naturalization certificate of his mother, who arrived in the U.S. as a 2-year-old, behind his desk in the Capitol. The DREAM Act, he said, has been his top priority “because it’s so personal.”

“These are real lives. Real people,” he said.

On the Senate floor over the years, he has recounted the details of more than 150 dreamers with the notion that people — even senators — respond more readily to stories than stump speeches.

And even with time quickly running down, a Republican-controlled Congress and an administration that has repeatedly cracked down on all forms of immigration, Durbin is still looking for deals to finally make the DREAM Act reality.

It’s a long shot, but the path for the DREAM Act has never been straightforward.

A prodigy’s future in limbo

Durbin first introduced what would become the DREAM Act in 2001, after instructors from the Merit School of Music in Chicago contacted his office about the obstacles faced by one of their standout students.

Lee was born in Brazil to South Korean parents and came to Chicago when she was 2 years old. Her father was a Presbyterian minister, and Lee began playing piano in his church at age 7. She taught herself hymns and classical pieces, and by the time she graduated from Lane Tech College Prep High School, Lee was taking more formal lessons at the Merit school and won a contest to play a piece — Tchaikovsky’s Piano Concerto No. 1 — with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. Her teacher, Ann Monaco, asked Lee where she was going to college.

But Lee knew she lacked legal status, so she told Monaco she “was not going to college.”

“She became the first person I told — ever — that I was undocumented,” Lee told the Tribune. “Back then, the term was, ‘I’m an illegal alien.’ From there, Ann asked me, ‘Do you trust me?’ I said, ‘Yes, I do.’”

Monaco took a variety of steps to try to help Lee, even exploring the possibility of adopting her. Eventually, Monaco connected her to Durbin’s office.

“Hers was a great story,” Durbin said, “and it illustrated an injustice in this country. Why in the world would you make her responsible for the fact that her parents didn’t file the right papers when she came to the country? Why would you hold her responsible for being from a poor family … struggling through public schools and excelling in music to the point where the Merit music program … ends up calling us and saying, ‘Can you help? This is a special case. She’s going to be a superstar. Give her a chance.’”

“It turned out the laws of America didn’t give her any chance at all,” Durbin said. To receive legal immigration status, Lee would have had to leave the country for 10 years and then apply to come back. Durbin thought that was unacceptable: “So I thought this was worth fighting for.”

Highlighting Lee’s story — and others like it — also made strategic sense, Durbin explained. As a House member, he helped pass a ban on smoking on commercial flights, and the lessons of taking on Big Tobacco stayed with him as he plotted a strategy on immigration.

“I reached a point where we were at a dead end with tobacco, because the argument was: ‘Durbin, listen, we know it’s bad, but these are grown-ups who are making this bad decision. It’s stupid for them to do it, but why the hell should we pass a law to stop them from doing it if they want to do something stupid? What’s next? No beer? No alcohol?’” he recalled.

“The way to transition it was children,” Durbin said. “When you start talking about marketing to children and the fact that 29% of kids in high school were smokers, you say to yourself, ‘These aren’t adults; these are kids. These companies know it, and they are advertising to these kids.’ So the issue of immigration has always been with us. … But when it comes to helpless kids being brought as infants to the United States and their parents making a bad decision or no decision that jeopardizes their lives after they’ve done everything that they’re supposed to do, that’s just plain wrong.”

Durbin quickly ran into another problem. Just four days after he introduced his proposal to help kids like Lee — a measure he called the Children’s Adjustment, Relief, and Education (CARE) Act — U.S. Sen. Orrin Hatch, a Republican from Utah, unveiled remarkably similar legislation but with a catchier acronym: the Development, Relief, and Education for Alien Minors (DREAM) Act.

Hatch was “angry as hell” that Durbin was taking his idea, Durbin said, so they hammered out a compromise and, because Republicans controlled the Senate, agreed to let Hatch be the lead sponsor of their joint proposal.

The bipartisan duo quickly built support and set a hearing for Sept. 12, 2001. Lee was scheduled to testify. She remembers Durbin and his team being optimistic it could pass the Senate.

But the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks upended those plans, with repercussions that are still felt today.

“Immigrants,” Lee said, “became the scapegoat.”

Grand bargains fall short

In the years following the 2001 attacks, Congress focused its attention on clamping down on immigration: creating the Department of Homeland Security, making driver’s licenses harder to get and beefing up the Border Patrol. When Hatch ran for reelection, he declined to co-sponsor the DREAM Act again, leaving Durbin to find the first of many other Republican co-sponsors.

Durbin then tried negotiating a grand bargain pairing tougher border restrictions with a path to legal status for immigrants without it. Though it led to some of the best odds for the DREAM Act’s passage, the compromise efforts fell short.

Durbin included the DREAM Act in a comprehensive immigration package that passed the GOP-controlled Senate in 2006 by a vote of 62-36. But the House, which also had a Republican majority, did not take up the measure.

The next year, a broader immigration package failed 53-46 in the Senate. Later in 2007, Durbin tried attaching the DREAM Act to a defense authorization bill, citing protections for immigrants who had served in the military. It won a 52-vote majority in the Democratic-controlled chamber but fell short of the 60 votes needed to break a Senate filibuster.

Meanwhile, dreamers increasingly drew attention to their situation by staging sit-ins at congressional offices, marching cross-country to Washington, or rallying at Chicago’s Federal Plaza chanting “undocumented and unafraid.”

After Obama moved to the White House, Democrats briefly controlled Congress, giving Durbin and Dream Act supporters their best chance to date to get the measure signed into law.

But the window for potential passage closed when Democrats lost control of the House amid the 2010 Tea Party backlash to Obama. In a lame-duck session beforehand, the House passed the DREAM Act 216-198.

When the legislation moved to the Senate, dozens of dreamers wore caps and gowns in the Senate galleries. But the bill died following a 55-41 vote, a clear majority but, again, not enough to defeat the filibuster.

At the Lutheran church in July, Durbin choked up recalling that day, Dec. 18, as he addressed dreamers who were again wearing caps and gowns.

“It was one of the saddest days I ever had as a congressman or a senator,” he told them. “Tears were shed by dreamers who thought this was their chance. And I told them, and I’ll tell you now: I’m not giving up on you. Don’t give up on me. We’re going to stick together through this, and we’re going to prevail.”

The origins of DACA

Even before the DREAM Act failed, Durbin had pressed the Obama administration to use its executive discretion to protect dreamers, drawing attention to their deportations in confrontations with Obama’s Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano during private meetings and Senate hearings.

Durbin tried to reach out to Obama directly. First, he sent a joint letter with U.S. Sen. Richard Lugar, an Indiana Republican whom Obama worked with during his time in the Senate, requesting an executive order. A year later, he sent a letter with 20 Democratic senators repeating the request.

“Then I sat down and talked to (Obama) personally” in June 2011, Durbin recalled. “It was an animated conversation because I was reporting on some things his administration was doing that he didn’t know. And he challenged me: ‘What do you mean we’re deporting dreamers?’ I said, ‘You are.’” Obama didn’t believe him, saying he checked out those claims, Durbin said. “I said, ‘I’ll give you the names.’ And I did. And he changed his approach shortly thereafter.”

Durbin said he thinks the conversation was “part of” what convinced the president — who had always supported the DREAM Act as a senator — to implement DACA. But Obama also faced resistance from within his own administration, whose members questioned his authority to make such a sweeping change, Durbin explained.

“He was there, and lives were saved because of it. He was showing leadership,” Durbin said of Obama.

On June 15, 2012, Obama formally created DACA. The program applied to people who arrived in the U.S. as children and had lived here more than five years, letting them apply every two years for protection from deportation and temporary work authorization if they paid a fee, passed a background screening and stayed clear of criminal charges.

Durbin and then-U.S. Rep. Luis Gutiérrez of Chicago decided to host an event at Navy Pier for interested families to learn more about the program. Durbin said they expected about 1,000 people to come. Instead, more than 11,500 attended and at least another 2,000 were turned away.

It was an eye-opening moment for Durbin and dreamers themselves.

“The thing about being undocumented is that you think you’re the only undocumented person to ever exist in the world, because it’s something that, growing up, you’re told not to share with anyone,” said Melanny Buitron, a dreamer who later interned in Durbin’s office. “So you can’t believe just how incredible — at least for me — it felt to know that I wasn’t the only one.”

She saw classmates in the same line at Navy Pier. Until then, she didn’t know they were undocumented.

Buitron said her prospects changed quickly.

“Before DACA, there was always this underlying uncertainty. … It was like my life was already chosen for me,” she said. “But when it came out, I’ll never forget when it did, because it was so life-changing. For the first time, I had the opportunity to dream. I was never really able to think ahead, to plan ahead, to think about who I wanted to be in life because of all these barriers.”

Still, it was a fraught moment. Her family spent their life’s savings hiring an attorney and paying the DACA application fee, Buitron said, worried about turning over so much personal information to the same government charged with deportations.

Those fears only grew once Donald Trump became president in 2017.

Digging in during the Trump era

“The very first time I met Donald Trump (was when) he was sworn in for his first term,” Durbin said. “I went to a luncheon, and he was sitting by himself at the head table. The new president, a few hours after being sworn in! And I went up to him, and I said, ‘I want to talk to you about the DREAM Act.’ And he said to me, ‘Oh, those kids. We’ll take care of it. Don’t worry about it, Senator.’ Well, it never happened.”

Durbin says much of the blame rests with Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who amassed more power in the White House during Trump’s second term than his first.

Miller, Durbin said, “truly, truly dislikes immigrants. It isn’t a question of security or safety; it’s cultural. He just believes we don’t want these people. ‘They don’t look like us. They don’t talk like us. They don’t eat our food.’ It’s a classic response to immigration we’ve seen throughout history.”

Indeed, the Trump administration tried to shut down DACA in 2017, months after coming into power. Legal challenges followed, leading to a 2020 Supreme Court decision that kept the program running. But shortly after Joe Biden became president, Texas and other Republican-led states sued to invalidate DACA on procedural grounds. As a result, no new applicants have been allowed to join, although renewals continue.

Last year, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, based in New Orleans, found DACA unlawful but limited its finding to Texas. The appeals court sent the case back to a trial judge to hash out how to implement the ruling. The trial court has not issued its ruling, though Durbin suspects the judge is holding off until after the midterms because a decision could be so disruptive.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has pursued dozens of DACA recipients for deportation as it steps up immigration enforcement across the country. In response to an inquiry from Durbin, the Department of Homeland Security acknowledged in February that it had arrested 261 DACA recipients and deported 86 of them, seemingly undermining the premise of the program.

The administration has also slowed DACA renewal processing, jeopardizing recipients’ work authorization. And because no new applicants are being allowed in, DACA now covers only a narrowing slice of the immigrant population — sometimes leaving younger siblings without the protections their older siblings have.

A profound impact

Tania Unzueta, political director for the Latino advocacy organization Mijente, is a Chicago-area dreamer who has fought for immigrant rights for as long as the DREAM Act has been around. She first garnered public attention in 2001, when she left the country to apply for an international student visa and was not allowed to return from Mexico. Durbin intervened, helping her return to Chicago, and she became a leader in the emerging undocumented youth movement.

She recalls making one of her first public remarks at a press conference with Durbin.

“I remember having my speech memorized. I remember trying not to make it about myself but the 65,000 undocumented students,” Unzueta said. “It was scary. I was nervous. I remember being very thankful.”

There was a point when Durbin was known to some as “Papa Durbin” for his role encouraging their advocacy, she recalled.

While Unzueta said she hasn’t agreed with Durbin on every immigration issue over the years, she said his championing of the DREAM Act “opened up room for people understanding that we could have rights.”

Pacheco, the president of TheDream.US, praised Durbin for pushing Obama and other Democrats in the Obama administration to take action.

“The key force in making DACA happen is Senator Durbin,” Pacheco said. “It’s his proximity to dreamers and his understanding of their plight, of what was happening across the nation.”

She blamed the DREAM Act’s failure to pass on strategic choices made by political leaders to avoid giving the other party a win.

“If you look at every time immigration has been put in the conversation, it’s always to benefit one party or the other, or to make one party or the other look bad,” Pacheco said. “They forget about the human beings and the people. It’s just a political issue.”

Jorge Loweree, managing director of programs and strategy at the American Immigration Council, said shepherding immigration-related legislation through Congress has become “extraordinarily complicated” since Durbin first unveiled the DREAM Act, as lawmakers now also grapple with asylum seekers, refugees, people who qualify for temporary protected status and border security.

“I think that Senator Durbin played a key role in crystallizing the issues confronting the dreamers — the fact that they exist, the issues they experience and why people should care about them,” Loweree said.

“Generally speaking, people in the U.S., irrespective of their political inclinations, if you ask them what a ‘dreamer’ is, the average person probably knows what you’re referring to,” Loweree said. “That certainly wasn’t the case before Senator Durbin decided to take up this mantle.”

Durbin said he doesn’t regret any of the tactical decisions he’s made trying to get the DREAM Act signed into law.

“Some things take awhile. You’ve got to be patient if you’re a senator,” he said. “You have to have the right moment, not only the right idea, but the right moment.”

The important thing is to keep the idea viable, he said.

“My goal is to pass the bill. But to pass the bill, you’ve got to keep it alive. We’ve been on this bill for 25 years. There are a lot of ideas that couldn’t last five. This one, I think, has been solid for a long period of time,” he said.

Durbin has been heartened by growing attention to immigration from the faith community, particularly Pope Leo XIV and the Roman Catholic Church, and he continues lobbying his GOP colleagues. He thinks he can count on four to six Senate Republicans who would support the measure now, and thinks more could be persuaded if it’s packaged with other immigration reforms. His last conversation with the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham was about passing the DREAM Act, he said.

U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, a Democrat whose district stretches from Chicago to the western suburbs, has worked with Durbin on immigration-related issues since she joined Congress in 2023. She attended a news conference with Durbin in mid-July after she became one of the first House members to sign a discharge petition trying to bring the DREAM Act to an immediate House vote, over the objections of House Republican leaders.

But Ramirez says her connection to Durbin is deeply personal. In 2020, while she was a state lawmaker and at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, Ramirez married Boris Hernandez, a DACA recipient — meaning that, until Hernandez received a green card last year, she was the only member of Congress married to a DACA recipient. Durbin’s success in convincing Obama to implement DACA changed her husband’s life, she said, allowing him to go to college and work in early childhood development.

“He and I were talking about who he wanted to officiate the wedding, and you know what he said? He said, ‘I want Dick Durbin to officiate our wedding because he has meant that I get to live without fear, and I got to meet you because I have more freedom — freedom to be me, freedom to be on social media, freedom to be working, freedom to go to school,’” she said. Durbin wasn’t able to preside over the ceremony because of his Senate schedule, but he sent a video they played during the wedding.

“I think of that video often. I think about how much that meant for Boris, who’s now 41 years old. They’re not kids anymore. They’re grown people with children, with businesses,” she said.

She said she hopes supporters of the DREAM Act can find four more House Republicans to sign the discharge petition, which could trigger a vote on the legislation and maybe, just maybe, get the DREAM Act to the president’s desk. Ramirez hopes Trump might be persuaded to sign it because he likes to take credit for big ideas.

“What a beautiful, full-circle moment that would be for a senator — that I know the last year has received some pushback and some critiques — to be able to say, ‘I end my time in Congress having passed the Dream and Promise Act,’” she said.

The Chopin piece Lee played at the church in July has been reworked into a melancholy song called “I’m Always Chasing Rainbows,” sung by Judy Garland and many others over the years, with lyrics bemoaning dreams “ending in the sky.” But Lee strikes a more optimistic note. “I do believe that dreams really do come true, if we work towards and fight for (them),” she said.

Lee has seen that change firsthand. Her parents fled Korea in the aftermath of the Korean War, then left Brazil after a family member robbed them. Her mother had to sell her wedding ring and jewelry to buy plane tickets and secure visas to the U.S. When Lee was a child in the U.S., a wealthy church parishioner gave her family beds, desks and — crucially — a piano because they were so poor.

But now Lee has a doctoral degree in music, and her dissertation focused on six composers who immigrated to the U.S. She is a mother and a U.S. citizen through marriage. In February, Durbin invited her to be his guest at the State of the Union address.

Durbin has encouraged her through the good and the bad, she said.

“He kept saying, ‘Don’t lose hope,’” Lee recalled. “He brought hope to thousands if not millions of undocumented immigrants.”

Daniel C. Vock is a freelancer.

authors: VALERIE GONZALEZ and CYBELE MAYES-OSTERMAN The Associated Press

"The combination of collapsed lead times and packed hearing blocks is a schedule designed for people not to have their case heard," said Bartlomiej Skorupa, chief operating officer of Mobile Pathways.

text:
HARLINGEN, Texas -- The Trump administration is packing immigration courtrooms and giving less lead time on hearings in an effort to clear a decades-long backlog. The result is a historic rise in the number of people missing court dates and being immediately ordered deported as the system struggles to keep up, new data shows.

Dozens and often hundreds of immigrants' cases a day are being assigned to individual judges in courthouses across the country, in what are known as "mega" master hearings, which have seen a significant increase this year. More than 1,300 such hearings were held in June alone, a nearly threefold jump from the previous June, according to data analyzed by Mobile Pathways, a nonprofit that tracks immigration court data to help immigrants, their lawyers and other organizations.

At the same time, the data shows, courts have severely cut the length of time many people are getting to prepare for complex immigration proceedings, from about six months to often just a little more than a month.

They're subsequently missing hearings, receiving deportation orders and being told they've abandoned any asylum claims at unprecedented rates.

"The combination of collapsed lead times and packed hearing blocks is a schedule designed for people not to have their case heard," said Bartlomiej Skorupa, chief operating officer of Mobile Pathways. "The data shows valid claims are closed before being adjudicated."

Those who favor stricter immigration laws see the swift hearings as a course correction for a longstanding problem.

"There's no credibility in the system that never reaches an end," Andrew Arthur, a fellow at the conservative Center for Immigration Studies, said.

Still, he worries that these rapid-fire hearings could affect judges' performance.

"You don't want to put so many cases on that the judges get burned out or that there's a danger of denying due process to anybody," Arthur said.

The Justice Department office that handles immigration courts said in a statement that judges were adjusting their schedules to resolve cases more quickly, while making sure all cases get handled fairly and lawfully. It said court delays harm immigrants who have valid claims, and that the public interest is served when the government deports people without legal grounds to stay.

IMMIGRATION COURTS OVERWHELMED

Attending immigration court in Harlingen on days when there are mega master hearings can mean waiting outside in the hot, crowded entrance for over an hour until the lobby can accommodate the next wave of people. Adults with cases often are accompanied by relatives and attorneys, and detained children are brought in with shelter case managers and legal advocates.

The courts call it a "mega" day when a judge has more than 50 cases scheduled. Although the practice is not new, it became much more frequent starting in mid-May.

On a recent day, about 90 cases were scheduled with Immigration Judge Delia Gonzalez. More than 20 people did not show up, but even so she ran out of time to hear each case and rescheduled a handful of people who had waited more than eight hours.

"There's a real limit to how many cases a judge can hear with any care in one morning," said former immigration judge Elizabeth Young. "When you cram that many hearings into a single docket, you're working through a list, not holding court."

Some immigrants requested more time before their next hearings, presenting evidence of having been defrauded by unscrupulous attorneys profiled in local news reports. Others without any attorney asked for more time to figure out the proper evidence filing procedures.

A Colombian man who submitted more than 1,500 pages as evidence in his asylum claim said he still wanted to obtain more documentation from members of the military, businesses and politicians back home.

Gonzalez declined the requests. Most cases lasted less than five minutes.

NO LEEWAY FOR NO-SHOWS

That same day in West Valley City, Utah, Immigration Judge Brock Taylor was assigned 159 cases. By noon, Taylor recited a dozen names of people from Mexico, Colombia, Peru and Venezuela who failed to show up. Without elaborating, he said each was properly notified of their hearing date and failed to appear. He ordered them removed from the United States and they would have no right to appeal.

In Chicago, attorney Peter Meinecke, a lawyer for the Resurrection Project, which runs a legal clinic for immigrants, said one of his clients was issued a removal order when he couldn't attend a mega master hearing across the country in Seattle after a vehicle accident fractured both of his legs and confined him to a wheelchair.

At the start of the second Trump administration in January 2025, about 20% of people missed scheduled immigration court hearings nationwide, according to Mobile Pathways. As hearing notice times shrunk, that no-show rate doubled to 40% by this June, the organization said.

Deportation orders have risen alongside the no-show rates. Almost 33,000 deportation orders were issued in January 2025. This June, there were about 79,000, according to Mobile Pathways' data. And once a deportation order is issued, an immigrant's asylum claim is almost always considered "abandoned."

The national rate of cases considered abandoned is now nearly five times the historical average dating back to 2009; in New York and Chicago specifically, it's roughly six times higher, according to Mobile Pathways.

"That's a recipe for disaster, because more people are going to be ordered removed in absentia who truly have a valid case," said Katie Fleming, a director at Acacia Center for Justice, a network of legal service providers.

Some people have even been issued deportation orders while they were inside the building that houses the Chicago immigration court, but were confused about where to go and how to get help, according to Alex McGriff, an attorney for the National Immigrant Justice Center, which runs a legal help desk there.

"The court ordered them removed despite the fact that they were not absent," McGriff said.

BACKLOG SHRINKING, CASELOADS ARE NOT

Advocates for stricter immigration policies call the strategy a time-saver.

"It really is economizing the judge's time," said Arthur, the Center for Immigration Studies fellow. "It is increasing the number of final orders that are going out, so that's decreasing the backlog entirely."

The backlog, which grew significantly under the Biden administration, has decreased for the first time in at least 10 years. The number of pending cases with the Executive Office of Immigration Review, which oversees immigration courts, decreased from 3.7 to 3.5 million in fiscal 2025 and continued to drop this year.

"It can be a tough job when you're doing it at scale," Arthur said.

Attorneys representing immigrants have similar challenges keeping up as their own caseloads intensify.

Jaime Diez, a veteran immigration attorney based in Brownsville, Texas, recently had almost 20 cases called in one day, nearly 10 times his previously normal pace.

"Due process is being thrown out of the window," Diez said standing outside the courtroom with a 6-inch-thick file for one client. "It's very worrisome. I don't know how long it's going to last."

Information for this article was contributed by Elliot Spagat of The Associated Press.

title: ICE must not be shielded from accountability | Letter - Sun Journal
description:
Agencies like ICE and local police have strict guidelines for pursuits and use of force.
Asking whether those were followed in a dangerous situation isn’t “disrespecting authority.” It’s just making sure everyone stays safe.
Security experts have said for years that technology and focused enforcement do a better job than a giant physical barrier.
They didn’t want any part of government — law enforcement included — to operate without oversight.
Following the law isn’t just something the public has to do.
text:
A letter to the editor by Duane Dumont of Leeds raises some real concerns (“I blame the Democrats and the media for ICE killing,” July 24) , but pointing fingers at the media or local officials skips over something pretty basic: law enforcement still has to follow its own rules.

Agencies like ICE and local police have strict guidelines for pursuits and use of force. Asking whether those were followed in a dangerous situation isn’t “disrespecting authority.” It’s just making sure everyone stays safe. Respect doesn’t disappear when we ask questions.

And we should stick to what’s actually true about national policy. Saying Vice President Harris “let millions” through the border doesn’t line up with how the system works. Her role was focused on diplomacy and the root causes of migration in Central America. Border operations fall under the Department of Homeland Security, and it continued enforcing federal law throughout that period.

Same thing with the fencing vote back in 2006. Supporting targeted fencing isn’t the same as backing a 2,000‑mile wall. Security experts have said for years that technology and focused enforcement do a better job than a giant physical barrier.

Our Founders built checks and balances for a reason. They didn’t want any part of government — law enforcement included — to operate without oversight. Following the law isn’t just something the public has to do. It’s something the people enforcing it have to do too.

Donald Cailler

Gardiner

In his op-ed last Sunday, Rep. Donald Ardell (“Assess ICE instead of trading blame,” July 24) sounds like he worked 25 years as a federal criminal investigator with integrity and is proud of his career.

That was then. This is now. And now is a very different time.
